#987. Can maths survive AI? Fields medallist Terence Tao calls for a ‘Maths 2.0’ world

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Terence Tao is a mathematician at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Advanced artificial-intelligence models are transforming mathematics at an astonishing speed. In the past few months, AI-aided proofs — logical arguments that demonstrate why a mathematical result is correct — have been released for hundreds of long-standing maths problems.

Mathematicians might need several months to fully understand the underlying arguments and implications of these automatically derived solutions. As a mathematician who uses AI tools for my own research, I can see that the field has fundamentally transformed. We now urgently need to establish a ‘Maths 2.0’ era, in which ‘proof scarcity’ is no longer a defining feature of the field.

How AI is reshaping discovery in maths and physics

How AI is reshaping discovery in maths and physics

The challenges associated with this new way of doing maths are already evident. Many AI-generated results are not described clearly enough to meet quality standards for publication. Some researchers using AI tools simply move on to the next problem once they have a minimally presentable proof, leaving results that can be difficult for other mathematicians to assess. And it still remains unclear how extensively AI models are drawing on the previous work of mathematicians without providing proper attribution.

The centuries-old practice of openly sharing maths problems is under serious threat because mathematicians are increasingly fearful that disclosing their research directions will lead to their work being ‘scooped’ by a rival who is equipped with a frontier AI model. Graduate students and junior mathematicians used to develop their skills and gain early recognition from their peers by solving such problems. On 6 October, technology firm OpenAI dumped hundreds of solutions to such problems online in one go. It disrupted countless research programmes overnight.

Perhaps the most counter-intuitive consequence is that human understanding of mathematics is falling behind, because AI systems generate results faster than mathematicians can digest and absorb them. Confined to pure mathematics, this ‘proof indigestion’ might be a minor concern. But AI-generated mathematical models deployed in the real world without a matching understanding of their mechanisms could have serious consequences. For example, complex AI-generated models are already used to some extent to determine who qualifies for a bank loan and to measure financial risk in markets. If the complexity of these models outpaces the capacity for humans to understand when they might malfunction, the risks of unforeseen mistakes will grow, affecting the general public.

‘It is incredible’: How AI is transforming mathematics

‘It is incredible’: How AI is transforming mathematics

These negative impacts are not inevitable. Used creatively, and with the right incentives, AI tools could enhance human understanding. It is still possible to change course, through a radical reassessment of the conventional incentive structure of mathematics and by introducing more-responsible practices around AI use.

#964. Author or artificial intelligence? Literature in crisis

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

AI is a hot topic at this year's Frankfurt Book Fair. An international literary scandal has raised questions about machine-generated texts.

It's the hot-button topic at the Frankfurt Book Fair: How profoundly will artificial intelligence (AI) transform the book industry, and how can this transformation be regulated?

Given the warnings about the technology's long-term risks to humanity as a whole, such debates might appear rather narrow in scope. In reality, however, they concern very concrete issues — copyright protection, the power of tech giants and the future of creativity. Many agree that the political measures taken don't go far enough.

This year, however, another aspect has entered the debate: Can we actually recognize when a text has been written with the help of artificial intelligence, and if so, can this be proven?

These are some of the questions raised by the current scandal surrounding Haitian-Canadian author Thelyson Orelien and his debut novel, "C'etait ca ou mourir," (This title means "It Was Either That or Die" in English but an English translation has not yet been published), which was published in Canada in the spring.

The book about global migration was universally acclaimed, with translation rights sold in more than 20 languages. Soon after the book was published in France, it was long-listed for the prestigious Prix Goncourt.

But then, all of a sudden, allegations emerged that the book had been written almost entirely using AI. Orelien, a rising literary star, found himself branded a fraud despite denying all the allegations. His nomination for the Goncourt was withdrawn.

So, who should we believe? An author or an AI that claims to have identified AI-generated writing?

"We will have to learn to live with doubt," said Hannes Bajohr, a professor of German literature at the University of California, Berkeley.

Bajohr has spent years examining how AI is changing both writing and reading. His prediction: If the origins of texts can no longer be reliably established, we will have to evaluate them differently. What matters will be their quality alone, rather than whether AI was used in the writing process.

Nina George, a bestselling author and the honorary president of the European Writers' Council, is unwilling to accept this.

At the Frankfurt Book Fair, she was awarded the Friedrich Perthes Prize in recognition of her commitment to issues such as AI and copyright reform.

George has addressed the European Parliament and the lower house of the German parliament, speaking and writing tirelessly about the dangers of AI models. It is perverse, she said, that an author should suddenly have to prove that their writing is the creation of a human. The focus of her campaigns are the tech corporations' self-serving mentality and copyright protection.

But what if an author sees AI not as an enemy but as a tool that makes writing easier?

US author and artist Luke Stoffel deliberately used AI in his memoir, "How To Win One Million Dollars and Shit Glitter," and was open about doing so.

"I'm dyslexic," he said in a video interview. "I've always written and made up stories, but I never dared to take them any further."

It was only with the help of AI, he said, that he was able to fulfill his dream. The technology drew his attention to weaknesses in his writing and suggested a marketing strategy that actually worked.

In May 2026, he received an award from the Independent Book Publishers Association for the book.

For South African author Coral Hart, AI is actually the foundation of her business model. Publishing under various pseudonyms, each year she releases more than 200 different novels, spanning the genres of romance, thriller and mystery.

Hart sees herself as an ideas person, as well as an editor and publisher. Although none of her books has yet become a bestseller, the business is profitable, she said, adding that each book reaches more than 5,000 people.

Stoffel considers the entire debate hypocritical and points out that many publishers have been working with AI tools for some time. He's certain that "right now, a million-copy bestseller is being printed that was created with the help of AI. The author won't admit it, and then there'll be a scandal."

It is entirely possible that the scandal surrounding Thelyson Orelien is precisely that story. But we may never know for sure.

For now, the battle against the tech giants continues, some of which are themselves increasingly concerned about losing control.

At the very start of the Frankfurt fair, the German Publishers and Booksellers Association issued an appeal to policymakers in Berlin and Brussels, calling for stricter regulation of artificial intelligence, which they said is more urgent than ever. More than 140 publishers have signed it.

But for now, it remains just an appeal. And the question of what authors themselves should be permitted to do with AI will undoubtedly continue to fuel debates in the future.

#951. 'Ragebait' is the 2026 German Youth Word of the Year

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Already named the 2025 Oxford Word of the Year, "rage bait" has also been widely adopted in German slang.

The 2026 Youth Word of the Year, "Ragebait," was announced on Saturday at the Frankfurt Book Fair by publisher PONS Langenscheidt.

The "Jugendwort des Jahres," or German Youth Word of the Year, is an annual campaign that documents the popularity of new slang expressions.

"Ragebait" (in English: rage bait) refers to social media content that is deliberately designed to make people angry, frustrated or morally outraged.

It aims to drive engagement, since the algorithms of platforms like Instagram, TikTok and X reward high-energy interaction. A post that generates a heated debate through angry comments, or that is widely shared due to the emotional reaction it provokes, counts as high engagement, which leads the platforms to push the content to more feeds.

"Ragebait" was on a shortlist of three words for the 2026 Youth Word of the Year, alongside "Peak" and "Crashout."

All three terms are borrowed from English, demonstrating once again the language's significant influence on German youth culture.

Around 1 million young people, aged 11 to 20, have voted since August 28 for their favorite term.

"Ragebait" obtained 36.5% of the votes, followed by 33.8% for "Peak" and 29.7% for "Crashout."

"The close result shows that all three terms have a firm place in the vocabulary of generations Z and Alpha," said Artur Raiser, marketing manager at PONS Langenscheidt, in a press statement. "'Ragebait' held a slight lead from the start," but only by a narrow margin throughout the voting period, he added.

"It remained an exciting race for us at the publishing house, too, until the very last moment," said Raiser

"Crashout" (used by young Germans as "crashout gehen," or "going crash out") originally comes from the English "to crash out," which traditionally means to fall asleep very quickly due to exhaustion.

But in newer internet slang, popularized on gaming and social media platforms, "crashing out" means having an intense emotional breakdown, losing control of one's temper or reacting with sudden, uncontrolled anger or stress. It is often used with a touch of humor, to emphasize that the reaction might be somewhat exaggerated.

As for the other shortlisted word, "Peak," it refers to something that is the absolute best. In German youth slang, it functions like an adjective: "That was peak football" or "that is peak comedy."

PONS Langenscheidt, a publishing company that specializes in language reference works, has been selecting the German Youth Word of the Year since 2008 — originally via a jury, and since 2020 through an online vote. Offensive, racist or discriminatory terms are not permitted. The multi-stage public nomination and voting process for next year's word will start in the summer of 2027.

"Das crazy" was selected last year, while "Aura" was the Youth Word of the Year 2024.

#949. A first for CRISPR: powerful prime editing alters DNA directly in the human body

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

The method called prime editing can make fine-scale edits to DNA (artist’s illustration).Credit: Patrick Landmann/Science Photo Library

A powerful gene-editing technique has been used to edit DNA directly in a person’s body — the first known instance of such a treatment.

The milestone treatment is part of a clinical trial of prime editing, a technique that can alter DNA with more precision than standard CRISPR–Cas9 methods can. In this case, prime editing was used to treat a condition called Wilson’s disease by rewriting DNA in liver cells, to erase a mutation that prevents them from eliminating excess copper.

Prime Medicine, a biotechnology company in Cambridge, Massachusetts, announced that it had treated the first person in its trial earlier this month. It expects to announce the first results from the study next year.

Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors

Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors

“I never dreamed that in my lifetime I would see this applied to my rare disease,” says Rhonda Rowland, president of the Wilson Disease Association in Atlanta, Georgia. “It’s going to be a really exciting year.”

In launching the trial, Prime Medicine joins a host of companies aiming to engineer cells directly in the body, rather than using the standard method of extracting a person’s cells, editing their DNA in a laboratory and then reinjecting the altered cells. Rewriting DNA in the body, or in vivo, is appealing because manufacturing and administering the treatment might be much cheaper and faster than making a bespoke therapy for each person from their own cells.

But in vivo approaches have their own challenges, says Krishanu Saha, a biomedical engineer at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. “It depends on what types of risks you’re willing to accept,” he says.

Wilson’s disease is caused by mutations in a gene called ATP7B, which encodes a protein that transports excess copper out of the liver. If left untreated, the resulting build-up of copper can cause liver and nerve damage, as well as neurological disorders.

People with Wilson’s disease are eager for a one-and-done treatment for their condition, says Rowland, rather than the current, complicated regimen of copper-clearing molecules and other medicines. And gene editing could, in theory, provide a lasting solution by correcting the faulty ATP7B gene.

So far, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved only one gene-editing therapy, called Casgevy, which is used to treat two inherited blood disorders. Casgevy relies on CRISPR–Cas9 gene editing, which is often used to disable genes rather than to rewrite their sequences.

Bizarre CRISPR enzyme kills cancer cells by shredding their DNA

Bizarre CRISPR enzyme kills cancer cells by shredding their DNA

Another form of gene editing, called base editing, can rewrite individual DNA letters, but cannot make the particular corrections needed to fix the most common ATP7B mutations. That left prime editing, a more complex and versatile system that can insert, delete and rewrite segments of DNA. In another clinical trial, Prime Medicine used the technique to treat two people with a rare immune disorder, by rewriting DNA in each participant’s blood stem cells outside of the body and then injecting them back in.

So far, no gene-editing therapies have been approved for use in vivo. But the FDA is expected to issue a decision early next year about an in vivo CRISPR–Cas9 therapy for a condition called hereditary angioedema, which causes severe swelling.

#942. German 'lawfare': When lawsuits become a political weapon

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

The Left Party is suing two government ministers for accusing them of antisemitism, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz has been sued several times by various parties. Is German politics descending into "lawfare?"

A verbal slip, an attempted quip, a lawsuit: Things can move fast in the rancorous atmosphere that currently rules German politics.

The brief exchange happened on a political TV talk show shortly after the Berlin election on September 20, won by the socialist Left Party. The show's host, Maybrit Illner, quickly corrected herself after accidentally saying of the Left Party's Berlin mayoral candidate, "Elif Eralp says she is an antisemite…. She is not an antisemite."

One of her guests, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), responded immediately: "Na doch" (or, "well, yes she is"). In the angry fallout, the Left Party's lawyers jumped on these two words, and have filed a lawsuit, arguing that this amounted to defamation of Eralp, as it falsely suggested that the Left Party politician did indeed consider herself antisemitic.

Not only that, the suit stated, Dobrindt's remark would "undermine her integrity as a political officeholder" and hinder her attempts to form a government in Berlin.

It was not the first time the Left Party has got its lawyers involved following its election victory, as it gets bombarded by accusations of antisemitism from the center right, especially over an incident at an election campaign event in Berlin when a rapper chanted "Death to the IDF" — the Israel Defense Forces, or the Israeli army.

Economy Minister Katherina Reiche also angered the socialist party by giving a speech in which she said that the party was now "openly embracing antisemitism." A video of the speech was posted on the Economy Ministry's Instagram account.

The lawsuit has become an increasingly popular weapon in German politics in recent years, usually by deploying sections 185, 186 and 187 of the German Criminal Code, which cover offenses including insult, defamation and "intentional defamation," which means knowingly asserting or disseminating untrue facts about others. Theoretically, the punishment can be a fine or up to a year in prison.

In September 2025, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) pressed defamation charges against Chancellor Friedrich Merz after he said that the far-right party's policy of remigration amounted to "ethnic cleansing."

Similarly, the Green Party in Berlin brought hate speech charges against Merz last year, when he said "we still have this problem in the cityscape" when describing the presence of immigrants.

In another case, the Green Party's own Robert Habeck was sued in 2024 by the Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) for claiming that the new upstart party was "buying votes" on the internet by building up "troll armies." Prosecutors dropped the case after Habeck agreed to pay €12,000 ($13,500) to three charities without admitting any wrongdoing, on the grounds that there was only limited public interest in a criminal procedure.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But charges like these, especially when politicians claim defamation, have little chance of success. "Prosecutors usually dismiss such cases very quickly due to a lack of sufficient grounds for suspicion," media lawyer Christian Solmecke, of the firm WBS Legal, told DW in an email.

"The Federal Constitutional Court has consistently held that, in the political arena, the boundaries of what is permissible are significantly wider than in the private sphere," Solmecke added. "Anyone who voluntarily enters the political arena must also be prepared to endure sharp, polemical, exaggerated and hurtful criticism."

Felix Zimmermann, editor-in-chief of the legal affairs outlet Legal Tribune Online (LTO), agrees, because German law makes a careful distinction between an opinion and a false statement. "'Antisemitic' or 'not antisemitic' is an opinion, especially at the moment, when people have very different definitions of it," Zimmermann told DW.

That hasn't deterred politicians from trying it more and more often. "We are undoubtedly observing a new level of intensity and scale of this practice," said Solmecke. "Political culture has become harsher and more polarized. The threshold for no longer merely engaging political opponents through debate, but instead outright criminalizing them, has dropped dramatically."

The danger, Solmecke argues, is that this often amounts to the "misuse" of law enforcement agencies as political instruments.

But lawfare appears to be effective as a political tactic, not least because it's a guaranteed headline. "From the point of view of the parties filing the complaints, they are highly effective as a PR strategy," said Solmecke. "The political benefit arises entirely independently of the legal outcome."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the Left Party's case, Zimmermann thinks it certainly pays to show you won't stand to be called antisemitic — not least because Eralp has repeatedly underlined her commitment to the Jewish community in Berlin.

"I think it's mainly about the fact that the Left Party wants to form a coalition in Berlin and Ms. Eralp wants to become mayor," Zimmermann said. "So of course it's good if you're insulted to challenge it, as a signal."

The motion against Katherina Reiche, on the other hand, may have much better chances — because she chose to post her inflammatory speech on the Economy Ministry's official social media channels. This could, Zimmermann said, well be seen as a violation of the "principle of neutrality," a constitutional rule that forbids the state from vilifying any particular political party.

"That is of course difficult for a politician, because if they say it on their own account, they're allowed, but if they say it on the ministry's account, they're not allowed," said Zimmermann. "It's a little absurd, because you're effectively splitting one person into two."

But even though the Left Party filed the complaint against Reiche as an urgent motion, the Constitutional Court may take several weeks, if not months, to actually decide the case — by which time the coalition negotiations in Berlin may have long since finished and Reiche's speech has had its effect.

The consequences for Reiche, in other words, will be limited — even if her ministry is forced to take down the post and the Left Party can eventually claim a victory.

#911. Moderna mRNA vaccine almost halves the risk of skin cancer returning

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Severe sunburn increases the risk of developing melanoma, the most serious type of skin cancer.Credit: Olga Pankova/Getty

A personalized mRNA vaccine reduced the risk of skin cancer returning or the recipient dying by 42% when used alongside an immunotherapy drug, according to long-awaited results for what could become the first approved mRNA vaccine for cancer.

Oncologists regard a risk reduction of 10% as substantial, says Kristen Radford, an immunotherapist at Mater Research in Brisbane. A risk reduction of more than 40% “would send many researchers over the Moon”, adds Seth Cheetham, a geneticist at the University of Queensland in Brisbane, Australia.

The personalized vaccine, called intismeran, is not designed to prevent skin cancer, or melanoma, from developing in the first place, but to stop it returning in people who have already undergone surgery to remove tumours.

Anticipation for the trial results has been building since August, when the vaccine’s developers — Merck, based in Rahway, New Jersey, and Moderna, which is headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts — announced early positive results. Data from the phase III trial will be presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology meeting in Madrid on 24 October. But when data were leaked online on 22 October, the companies released the key results.

The stock price for Moderna, a pioneer in mRNA vaccine technology, had been rising since the August announcement, but dropped by around 25% after the leak. Health-care financial analyst Evan Seigerman at BMO Capital Markets in New York City told media company Forbes that such reactions in the stock market probably reflect “inflated expectation into the full data release, rather than a true indictment on the efficacy of the combo therapy”.

The intismeran trial enrolled 1,137 people with moderate to advanced melanoma across 157 centres. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either a tailor-made vaccine (intismeran) alongside the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab — which is already used to treat melanoma — or pembrolizumab plus an inactive placebo. Trial leader Georgina Long, an oncologist at Melanoma Institute Australia in Sydney, says participants have so far been followed for around 25 months and will continue to be monitored for several years to determine whether the vaccine improves overall survival. She adds that the therapy did not result in any major harmful side effects.

Roughly 15 years ago, people with advanced melanoma typically survived for only months. Today, nearly 55% are effectively cured with targeted drugs or immunotherapies, says Long. The combination of intismeran and pembrolizumab is designed for people whose cancer could return after surgery and who do not respond to immunotherapy alone, she says.

Jessamy Tiffen, a cancer geneticist at the Centenary Institute in Sydney, says that the trial results are exciting, but that only time will tell how effective the treatment is beyond two years. “Cancer cells also have an insidious ability to adapt and evade whatever treatment we throw at them,” she says. Furthermore, some people did not respond to the vaccine, she says.

Long says that her team will conduct a statistical analysis to identify who is most likely to benefit from the treatment.

To develop intismeran, Long and her colleagues sequenced DNA from a sample of each participant’s tumour to identify mutations in the cancer cells. These mutations can give rise to proteins called neoantigens, which help to distinguish cancer cells from healthy ones.

#903. Pope lung nodule: Could it be cancer?

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

The case of Pope Leo shows how small lung nodules are often found during routine health checks. Quick treatment is generally advised before nodules can grow to become larger life-threatening masses.

It often takes a chest X-ray or CT scan to spot small lung (or pulmonary) nodules, especially when a patient is asymptomatic.

At less than 3 centimeters (1.1 inches), lung nodules are less likely to press against your airway and cause any chest pain or shortness of breath or wheezing.

In the case of Pope Leo XIV, who told a gathering at the Vatican on October 11, 2026, doctors had found a nodule on his lung, it is unclear exactly how large that nodule is.

All we know (at time of writing on October 12, 2026) is that it was "detected at a very early stage," and that it was "well localized."

That suggests it has not spread or metastasized, although its full status is not publicly known. Doctors advised the pontiff to have his lung nodule removed.

Whether his was a chance finding — or whether the pope had presented with symptoms — we do not know.

But "incidental findings of lung nodule(s) in asymptomatic individuals" is considered an "increasingly common clinical dilemma," according to a 2019 paper published in the Annals of Thoracic Medicine.

This "dilemma" rests in part on the fact that biopsies — removing a small sample of tissue from the spot or nodule to determine whether it's malignant (cancerous) — are difficult to perform on small nodules.

The risks involved in a surgical diagnosis are considered "excessive compared to the relatively low prevalence of malignancy in the small nodules."

That's according to a 2017 paper published in the European Respiratory Review. And that may also be the dilemma that Pope Leo's doctors have faced.

Fortunately many — if not most — early-stage lung nodules are benign. It is also possible to have more than one nodule at a time, and they can all be benign.

It's said the pope will need a week to recover after his operation to remove the lung nodule. He is due to travel to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru between November 6-17.

Lung nodules are generally defined as a white spot or lesion on the lung. They have a rounded or irregular shape.

Radiologists refer to their "opacity" because, compared to the surrounding air-filled lung tissue, lung nodules appear as white or gray spots on a CT scan — that is, they have a certain density.

Lung nodules can be caused by old lung infections, foreign particles that are inhaled and get lodged in the lung, inflammation, scar tissue and indeed the onset of cancer.

At more than 3 centimeters, the nodule is defined as a mass. The bigger it gets, the greater the chance that it will obstruct your airway and the lung's ability to function.

Symptoms may start with chest pain, shortness of breath and wheezing. They may then progress to a chronic cough or coughing up of blood, fatigue, hoarseness, loss of appetite, unexplained weight loss and recurring respiratory infections like bronchitis or pneumonia.

It is hard to determine when lung nodules become life-threatening cancer. But one indicator of a lung nodule's malignancy is its size.

At 2 milimeters or smaller, the risk of cancer is very small and remains so up to a nodule size of about 6-7 milimeters.

The risk of cancer becomes 9%-10% at about 8 to 10 milimeters. And at larger than 1 centimeter, the risk of cancer is about 15%.

The density of a lung nodule is also a vital indicator of malignancy.

There are two main categories of lung nodule density: solid and subsolid. Subsolid nodules are further divided into pure ground-glass (nonsolid) and part-solid nodules.

According to a 2026 review article published in the New England Journal of Medicine, subsolid nodules are less prevalent than solid nodules, but they have "a higher likelihood of being malignant."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

It is said that radiologists see lung nodules in about 30% of chest CT scans. But that number may be rising.

A Dutch study published in 2023 cited an increase in lung nodule detections from 38% of scans in 2008 to 50% in 2019. The same study said "the proportion of patients in whom significant new nodules (≥ 5 mm) were reported increased from 9% in 2010 to 17% in 2017."

However, this may also be a result of the development of better scanning technology in recent years and the use of artificial intelligence to spot tumors.

Bearing in mind that most lung nodules are benign, lung cancer does tend to start with a lesion or nodule. And lung cancer remains the most common type of cancer and the most common cause of cancer death in the world.

The World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer says that in 2024 almost 2.65 million people were diagnosed with lung cancer and more than 1.8 million people died from the disease.

#876. First person infected with rare Shamonda virus: what we know

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Rachel Fieldhouse is a reporter for Nature in Sydney, Australia.

An outbreak of Shamonda virus was detected in cows in Europe in July and is ongoing.Credit: Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty

An individual with cancer in France has become the first person known to contract the Shamonda virus, after an outbreak in livestock in Europe that was first identified in July. The man, aged in his sixties, died on 9 October, 16 days after he started showing neurological symptoms, including vision loss and confusion, according to a case report published in Eurosurveillance this week1. Infectious-disease researchers say little is known about the virus or how it affects the body.

The man lived in a rural area in the Rhône–Alpes region, where Shamonda virus has been detected in cattle. He was probably infected after being bitten by midges, the report states.

It is also possible that he contracted the virus by eating contaminated food or through a blood transfusion or transplant, although the report’s authors say these routes are less likely. “Investigations are ongoing to rule them out,” they write. Researchers say that the risk of the virus being transmitted between people is low.

Shamonda virus belongs to a family of viruses called orthobunyaviruses, which are known to infect animals such as cows and deer, and are transmitted by mosquitoes and midges, says Krispin Hajkowicz, an infectious-disease researcher at the University of Queensland, Australia. There are no vaccines or antiviral treatments for orthobunyaviruses, Hajkowicz says.

More orthobunyaviruses are being detected in people, says Daniel Rawle, a virologist at the QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute in Brisbane, Australia. Climate change and greater contact between wildlife, livestock and humans are some of the factors that have increased the risk of people becoming infected. Another element is that a growing number of people are immunocompromised, and so more at risk of being infected and developing life-threatening symptoms. Although no human-to-human transmission has been recorded for these viruses, during an outbreak of an orthobunyavirus called Oropouche in Brazil in 2024, transmission was reported between pregnant women and their fetuses.

The individual in France, who had leukaemia and was severely immunocompromised, started having seizures shortly after the onset of symptoms and went into a coma, requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. When his symptoms did not improve after treatment with antibiotics, an antiviral drug and high doses of corticosteroids, he was taken off life support.

#853. The hidden treasure in discarded wearable and fast tech

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Sales of fast tech like mini fans and disposable e-vapes, as well as wearable health tech such as heart monitors and smartwatches are soaring. They're creating a new e-waste problem but are full of hidden treasure.

From mini fans and the cheap chargers to smartwatches bought as part of a New Year's health kick, some 44% of Europeans own at least six "fast-tech" gadgets. And more than half say they keep unused and broken e-waste items languishing at home or throw them in the regular trash instead of recycling.

That's according to a new report by Brussels-based e-waste association WEEE Forum. It describes fast tech, which is booming, as charging and lighting devices under €10 (circa $11), high-tech items like power banks and fitness trackers, and gadgets and lifestyle appliances like cheap mini blenders and fans, as well as single-use electronic vapes.

"So, these electronics are a bit like fast fashion," Magdalena Charytanowicz, WEEE Forum's Communication Manager, told DW.

Nearly 40% of buyers recalled discarding a fast-tech item without using it at all or within a month of buying it, and nearly 60% said they had used a product for no longer than six months. Yet the vast majority of respondents were generally satisfied with their gadgets despite short-lived functionality.

This suggests consumers accept the "fast-tech bargain" of poor quality that "does the job for a while" and is easily replaced — similar to fast fashion — according to the report.

About 62 million tons of electronics are discarded worldwide annually. "That's the Great Wall of China of e-waste that is produced every year," noted Charytanowicz, adding that the figure is set to grow to 82 million by 2030.

In Europe, roughly 40% of electronic waste is recycled, yet the rate worldwide is just 17%. This means valuable materials are lost, while electronic waste ends up polluting the environment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2022, a million tons of critical raw materials were embedded in the 10.7 million tons of e-waste generated across Europe, including manganese, gold, copper and aluminum.

These materials are at "the center of geopolitical tensions," Charytanowicz said, referring to escalating global tensions over access to rare earths and other critical minerals.

"Even the smallest" devices are worth recycling if they contain a circuit board or battery, she said.

Groups like WEEE Forum say more awareness raising is needed on how to dispose of cheap electronic devices, and that recycling should be made as easy as possible.

But the best way to reduce a product's environmental impact is to extend its lifespan through better design and repair, as recycling raw materials is energy intensive.

Charytonawicz said clearer, harmonized EU rules now under consideration could help improve e-waste collection. The bloc's 20-year-old directive is "not really adapted to the changing reality," she said.

Another growing area of e-waste is digital healthcare. While devices such as diabetes sensors and blood pressure monitors are "transforming healthcare," many are designed to be disposable.

A study published in Nature in December 2025 found sales of wearable healthcare electronics, for example, could reach 2 billion devices annually by 2050, and generate a million tons of e-waste.

Jeremy Faludi, associate professor of sustainable design engineering at TU Delft in the Netherlands, says making health tech — particularly digital devices used in, or issued by hospitals — recyclable or reusable comes with some "much bigger challenges" than normal electronics.

That's in part due to the potential for patient contamination, particularly with digital surgical devices that come into contact with blood or other bodily fluids.

"The way that a lot of things are designed now, you can't recover the stuff because it can't be easily sterilized without the electronics," said Faludi.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He worked on the Digital Health in Circular Economy (DiCE) project, an EU-funded initiative, to help redesign digital healthcare devices to "recover critical materials and reduce environmental impacts without compromising patient safety."

A modular design, for example, allows electronic components to be separated from the parts that need to be replaced between patients, making devices easier to reuse.

The four-year DiCE project, which included citizens, hospitals and manufacturers across nine EU countries, found reusable ECG cables — which connect patients to heart-monitoring equipment — cut environmental impacts by up to 81-94%, for example. The sets are usually designed for single use.

Rules around medical waste can also make reuse and recycling more difficult, particularly when requirements differ between countries and often come down to perceived rather than actual risk, Faludi added. He says some 85% of hospital trash is not infectious but everything ends up in the same bins. Better sorting as well as EU-wide regulations around treating non-infectious hospital waste would help here.

Like with other tech, consumer health devices such as blood pressure and glucose monitors often risk being forgotten in drawers or ending up in the wrong waste, simply because people do not know how to dispose of them, said Charytanowicz of WEEE Forum, which is also involved in DiCE.

Pilot schemes in Belgium, Spain and Slovenia that offered free postal returns and collection machines in public places found that more than 60% of people were willing to return unwanted devices if it was a straightforward process.

"What's really important is the convenience so that it can be integrated in your daily routines," said Charytanowicz, adding that "nudges" such as messages that recycling a device could help the health of another person motivate people to "do the right thing."

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remain at high risk of relapse despite perioperative treatment1-3. NeoCOAST-2 (NCT05061550), a phase 2, randomised platform trial, tested novel perioperative treatments in patients with stage IIA–IIIB NSCLC. At primary analysis, combining standard chemotherapy plus durvalumab (anti-PD-L1 antibody) with oleclumab (Arm 1, n = 76), monalizumab (Arm 2, n = 72) or datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd; Arm 4, n = 54) resulted in pathological complete response (pCR) rates of 20.3%, 25.7%, and 35.2%, respectively4. Here, we present the first report of prespecified secondary endpoints of event-free survival (EFS) and circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) clearance, and exploratory analyses of associations between ctDNA dynamics and clinical outcomes. The 24-month EFS rates were 70.5%, 75.7% and 77.9% in Arms 1, 2 and 4, respectively. Using a tumour-agnostic assay, ctDNA clearance at neoadjuvant Cycle 3 Day 1 was highest in Arm 4 (50.9%, 54.5%, and 72.5% in each arm, respectively). ctDNA clearance correlated with prolonged EFS versus non-clearance (pooled hazard ratio (HR) 0.22; 95% CI = 0.11–0.45, P = 0.0000443). Patients with both ctDNA clearance and pCR had favourable EFS outcomes versus those with neither (EFS HR 0.10, 95% CI = 0.02–0.42, P = 0.002). These findings suggest combined assessment of ctDNA clearance and pCR may improve risk stratification, and that the numerically highest pCR4 and EFS rates with the Dato-DXd combination warrant further evaluation.

#778. Brazil election: many scientists relieved as Lula wins surprise victory

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva celebrated on the evening of 25 October after coming from behind to win re-election as Brazil’s president.Credit: Maira Erlich/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won his bid for re-election on 25 October, to the relief of many scientists who feared for the future of Brazilian research if right-wing candidate Flávio Bolsonaro prevailed.

In recent weeks, some of Brazil’s leading scientific organizations, including the Brazilian Academy of Sciences in Rio de Janeiro, circulated an open letter endorsing Lula, a leftist former labour leader. It received more than 20,000 signatures. “It’s hard to express just how happy the scientific community and the Brazilian society is with Lula’s victory,” says Paulo Artaxo, a physicist at the University of São Paulo.

Science philanthropy is rising in Brazil ― upending a long tradition

Science philanthropy is rising in Brazil ― upending a long tradition

Many worried that, if Bolsonaro were elected, he might slash support for Brazilian science and undermine it in the way that his father, Jair Bolsonaro, did. Jair was Brazil’s president from 2019 to 2023, and during that time, he cut science funding and expressed anti-science rhetoric during the COVID-19 pandemic, casting doubt on vaccines and promoting unproven treatments. The former president could not run for office again because he was sentenced to prison over a coup plot that he instigated after he lost his bid for re-election to Lula in 2022. He is currently serving the sentence at home because of health concerns.

It was a surprise victory yesterday for Lula, who won 51.8% of the vote compared with Flávio Bolsonaro’s 48.2%. During the first round of voting on 4 October, Lula finished behind Bolsonaro, but because neither candidate earned 50% of the total votes, a second round of voting was required. “It was very moving to watch this historic turnaround,” says Sidarta Ribeiro, a neuroscientist at the Federal University of Rio Grande do Norte in Natal.

Lula’s victory came at the end of a tumultuous election day. Shortly before the polls were meant to close, a justice in Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered them to remain open for an additional two hours. The move was requested by both Lula’s and Bolsonaro’s campaigns because of public transportation problems that made it difficult for voters to reach polling stations. In a short speech yesterday, Bolsonaro said he would not accept the results.

This will be Lula’s fourth term overall as president of Brazil, a record for the country. He initially led Brazil for two terms between 2003 and 2011. During those terms and his current term, which started in 2023, he championed the expansion of federal universities and efforts to make higher education accessible to a broad range of Brazilians, support that he has pledged to continue. He also launched a program in 2024 that brought back about 600 Brazilian scientists to the country from international institutions, where some had gone seeking improved funding and resources.

“Lula said very clearly in his victory speech that we need to strengthen federal universities and federal institutes and significantly improve how we prepare young people for a new world of [artificial intelligence] and robotics,” Ribeiro says.

Supporters of Brazilian President Lula cheered in the streets of São Paulo on 25 October after it became clear that he had won his bid for re-election in a tight race.Credit: Rodrigo Paiva/Getty

Flávio Bolsonaro had pledged to transfer operation of Brazil’s 69 federal universities from the Ministry of Education to the Ministry of Science and Technology, which has a much smaller budget. In addition, he said he would emphasize applied sciences over basic research, which concerned some in the scientific community because “the countries that have made the greatest advances in science are those with an extremely strong foundation in basic research”, Ribeiro says.

Another major source of concern for some researchers about the election was the future of Brazil’s environmental policies. Under President Lula, deforestation in Brazil’s considerable portion of the Amazon rainforest fell to its lowest level since measurements began in 1988. Between 2019 and 2023, however, deforestation rose by almost 60% under Jair Bolsonaro, and a similar trend was expected under his son. The Amazon rainforest is considered one of the world’s largest carbon sinks, but studies suggest that increasing deforestation could cause it to release more carbon than it absorbs.

Meanwhile, Lula said during his recent campaign that he is committed to ending deforestation in Brazil by 2030, and that he would cut the country’s greenhouse-gas emissions in line with the Paris Agreement, which nations signed onto nearly a decade ago to curb climate change. “Lula’s government plan is very clear: he’ll work towards zero deforestation in the Amazon and towards implementing energy transition programs that end the use of fossil fuels in Brazil,” Artaxo says.

#766. Why Chinese tech brands are outpacing Western rivals from EVs to robot vacuums

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

From action cameras and smartphones to EVs and robot vacuums, Chinese brands are gaining ground worldwide, despite privacy and security concerns. What's driving their rise, and can European rivals keep up?

Do you remember the days when GoPro was synonymous with action cameras?

At its peak in 2015, the US company reigned supreme with around 6.6 million units sold that year and a market share of over 70%. Today, the pioneer is fighting for survival.

GoPro's biggest rivals, DJI and Insta360, entered the action camera market in 2019 and 2021, respectively. Today, they account for more than 90% of global smart handheld camera sales.

Alexander Hannemann, who regularly uses action cameras to film his motorcycle rides, says he switched from GoPro to Insta360 around two years ago.

"The quality is much better than a GoPro, even when I'm speeding up and going into corners at like 80 kilometers per hour," he told DW.

GoPro's case is not an exception. Since around 2010, many Chinese brands have not only caught up but surpassed once-dominant Western rivals across the consumer technology industry, from smart TVs to robot vacuums.

Gone are the days when "Made in China" stood for cheap, mass-produced products.

"China is still making affordable products today," says Chris Pereira, a Canadian entrepreneur and author with over 20 years of experience in China. "But the products are also high quality."

This combination has led to well over half of new consumer tech products globally coming from Chinese suppliers, Pereira adds.

BYD, Xpeng and other Chinese car manufactures sold almost two-thirds of all electric cars last year, surpassing incumbents like Tesla. In robot vacuums, Chinese brands dominate the global market, leaving former pioneer US company iRobot struggling to compete.

So why do Chinese companies increasingly outperform their Western rivals?

Pereira, whose consultancy iMpact helps Chinese companies gain traction overseas, attributes China's success to fierce domestic competition in cities like Shenzhen, Hangzhou and Shanghai; highly integrated supply chains and a can-do business culture that allows companies to innovate; and respond to problems quickly.

Other key reasons for China's competitive edge include unparalleled industrial automation, the strategic use of AI in manufacturing, responsiveness from regulators as well as relatively cheap labor, which together leads to significantly lower production costs and much faster innovation cycles than in the world's most advanced economies.

Joey Cheng, who moved to the US for his PhD studies over 20 years ago, is familiar with both the American consumer and the Chinese producer sides.

While his startup is based in the US, almost all the manufacturing is done in Shenzhen, where a large share of the world's hardware and consumer electronics are made.

"The supply chain in Shenzhen is basically inevitable for cost cutting and quick product development," Cheng says. "Especially as a startup you must get the product out quickly, or you'll get blown out of the water."

Although consumers are flocking to Chinese companies, some reservations persist.

A recent poll found that more than 90% of Europeans do not trust Chinese technology companies with their data, while about 80% distrust US firms. Germans expressed the highest level of mistrust.

Nadine, a German travel blogger who uses DJI and Insta360 products, says she wouldn't use any Asian products at home.

"My home robot vacuum is from a German company for precisely this reason: So the data remains compliant with German regulations. After all, manufacturers can connect directly to the camera," she said, referring to camera and audio hacking incidents involving robot vacuums.

Still, Pereira says that Chinese companies expanding abroad have to pay a "trust premium."

"This trust deficit means that they need to be extra competitive in terms of product and price in order for the market to choose them," he says, adding that the gap can be narrowed by a presence in overseas markets like BYD's first European passenger-car plant, expected to open in Hungary later this year.

Chinese companies say they comply with EU data protection rules. However, domestic security laws in the US and China can require firms to hand over data to authorities, and German officials note limited oversight of whether data is transferred from European servers abroad.

In addition to privacy concerns, Chinese consumer tech firms have come under scrutiny over espionage and other risks, most recently regarding connected devices like EVs.

In light of security concerns, trade deficits and China's overall dominance, the US and several other Western countries have hit Chinese imports and companies with tariffs, blacklists and strict requirements. In late July, the Trump administration banned the import of humanoid robots manufactured outside the US.

A representative of Chinese robot maker Primebot told DW that all Chinese consumer tech companies are feeling the effects.

"We might seek cooperation with a local US company. Another potential solution is building a factory there," he said.

European countries and the EU are also weighing more tariffs against Chinese companies.

Chris Pereira foresees that the tariffs will accelerate two trends among Chinese companies: Moving more manufacturing overseas and an increasing focus on challenging top-tier Western brands with premium goods.

"Chinese officials and companies recognize that manufacturing needs to be localized to a certain degree. One reason is to assuage the challenges of exporting, another is to create trust locally," Pereira sums up.

"The other trend is that once duties wipe out the price advantage at the bottom, the margin left is at the top, so Chinese brands are increasingly competing directly with established Western names, where trust matters most."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As China's dominance keeps growing, Western companies are scrambling to find ways to stay competitive.

Kaz Merchant, who works for a UK-based company that imports and exports IT hardware, says smaller companies, in particular, must carve out a geographic niche.

"They need to have their own unique selling point for a certain product, which China might not have for that region. Or they need to partner with a Chinese company," he says.

To Pereira, a key issue Europe needs to solve is regulators' responsiveness.

"Chinese regulators tell you very clearly and quickly what you can do. That speed helps companies iterate and succeed overseas," Pereira says.

"If you're waiting weeks for a response, you're going to lose business."

Dom Byrne is a freelance radio and podcast producer based in Brighton, UK.

Melanie Stefan says early career researchers can learn from others’ failures.Your browser does not support the audio element.Download MP3See transcript

Melanie Stefan leads a computational neurobiology lab at MSB Medical School Berlin. But as a postdoc 16 years ago, a failed fellowship application prompted her to write an article in Nature. In it, she called for researchers to keep a ‘CV of failures.’

Stefan says: “The idea would be that the successful people in science would actually open up about the failures that they had on their way, and how many jobs they didn’t get, how many positions they weren’t admitted to, how many grants they failed to receive, how many papers were rejected, things like that, so that younger scientists (like I was at the time) could actually take heart and see that this is actually a normal part of the process and that they’re not alone.

“So that was the idea. And since then, I’ve kind of become the poster child of failure a little bit.”

This is the second episode of a six-part podcast series about failure in science, pegged to a conference held in April at Imperial College London, in partnership with Nature.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03410-7

So I’m a chemist and experimental scientist, so I don’t need to search very hard for examples of day-to-day failure.

That’s Dr Alena Vdovchenko, a postdoctoral scientist at Imperial College London, talking in April this year at the Failure in Science conference.

In the lab, simply most of the things don’t work the way you plan them.

So sometimes you carefully design the experiment. You run it for sometimes weeks, months. It depends.

But then when you analyze the results, you realize that okay, you didn’t account for factor A.

You need to redesign the experiment, maybe read more literature, go back to the lab.

Alena was speaking at the session called A Taxonomy of Failure, where we heard early career researchers explaining how, in real life, (let’s put it like this), things often don’t go quite as planned.

But overall, I think a lot of chemistry is trial and error. And during my PhD, we have that quote printed in our lab.

Theory is when you know everything but nothing works.

Practice is when everything works but no one knows why.

In our lab, theory and practice are combined.

I feel like it’s very funny, but also very uncomfortably true.

I’m Dr Stephen Webster, director of the Good Science Project at Imperial College London, a programme that examines what we like about research culture, and what we don’t.

And in episode two, we hear panelist Melanie Stefan, professor of physiology at Berlin Medical School, talk about failure and the lab.

My first big experience of failure in science was when I was doing my masters in a developmental biology lab, and I really had a difficult time there.

I didn’t quite know how to troubleshoot experiments if they failed. I didn’t quite understand what I was doing. I think it was not the right place for me.

And the worst day was when my supervisor called me into his office and said, "Melanie, I think you should really look for jobs outside of science."

And that was devastating because I had been studying science for many years at the time. I saw myself as a scientist. I didn’t really have a Plan B.

So much of my identity was being a scientist and doing science.

Not just that I loved doing it, and I was really interested in it, but also I didn’t know what else I could do.

So this was really a devastating failure for me.

And I wrote an article about this in Nature. It’s also the only thing I have published in Nature.

Other journals exist, and since then I’ve kind of become the poster child of failure, kind of without intending it.

So at the Failure in Science conference at Imperial College, I talked about this article I wrote called A CV of Failures.

And the story of that is after my master’s degree, (which I ended up completing in the end), I did a PhD, and I had a very great time there.

I had a lot of fun. It was quite a successful time for me.

But then I was done with that, and I needed to apply for funding to go to the next stage of my career as a postdoc.

And it was really hard. It was really hard to find funding. And I was rejected from, a lot of my funding applications were rejected. I started doubting myself.

And I also thought that, "Oh my God, I’m the first person this has happenened to."

Because all the other scientists around me, obviously, or like the scientists who were like a bit further ahead they were further ahead because they were ultimately successful in securing a postdoc position.

And so all I saw around me was ultimately the successes.

So I felt like I was the only one who had ever failed. So that made it even worse, and so this gave me the idea of writing this article calling for a CV of failures.

So the idea would be that the successful people in science would actually open up about their failures that they had on their way, and how many jobs they didn’t get, how many positions they weren’t admitted to, how many grants they failed to receive, how many papers were rejected, things like that.

So that younger scientists like I was at the time could actually take heart and see that this is actually a normal part of the process and that they’re not alone.

So that was the idea. And since then, I’ve kind of become the poster child of failure a little bit.

A lot of friends tell me, "Oh, Melanie, I read something about failure. I was thinking of you."

I was like, "Thank you. That is so nice."

I think it’s generally really cool that there has been following up on this article a bigger discussion about failure in science that the conference was also part of.

I think that’s really lovely. And it’s really lovely to see people come together and talk about this concept.

The conference is called Failure in Science, but I’d like to smuggle in engineering. I know Mary already mentioned engineering in the last session, and I’m an engineer, and I think engineering has a very well developed tradition of understanding and learning from failure.

So I liked the the session that was called "A View from the Lab.

And it was especially nice to to hear from the more junior scientists about how they interacted with failure and how they experienced it.

But I also thought the moderator George Constantinides is one thing that really that I found really interesting about what he said was how he compared it to engineering.

And I think if I were to summarize the very broad literature on failure in engineering, at least my understanding is: number one, there is no failure without uncertainty.

And number two, structured ways from learning from failure are essential.

And I think those are things that we can carry forward into many different aspects of our work.

In general, I would kind of summarize by saying, in my view, if we want people to fly high, then we have to make it easy and safe to fail well.

And in engineering, you have to fail. Like, that’s how. You build something, you try a prototype and then it fails, and you learn from that.

You watch how exactly it failed, you analyze it, and then you build the next better version, and the next version, the next version.

And I think the point he was making, and I really agree with that, is that we should treat scientific careers in the same way, and that we need to give people spaces where it’s safe to try something and fail, and then to talk about it, and learn from it, and then do better the next time and try again.

And maybe fail in a different way, but then build something in the end that’s better. So I really like that engineering analogy.

So one thing that also came up in a lot of the discussions at the conference, and that I think is really important, is the question of who actually gets to talk about failure and who gets to fail.

So the reason why I’m invited to conferences like that is that ultimately I did finish my master’s degree, and ultimately I did become a scientist.

And this is why I get to talk about failure is in my scientific career is because ultimately I have succeeded.

And what about the people, though, who have failed?

But people who have set out to have a life in science and are now doing something else. We never hear from them, right, because they are not in that space anymore?

So I think it takes a certain amount of privilege and position to be allowed to talk about failure.

And also, when I was a young scientist and I was looking for positions, I was sometimes, like, googling my name, and then the first thing that came up was A CV of Failures.

And I thought that was really strategically not that clever of me.

But I was not in a position then where it was much less safe to open up about failures.

And now I’m in a position where I can do it because I have a professorship. Nothing is nothing bad is going to happen to me.

So this privilege of opening up about failure is really important.

And then also failure itself is something that you need quite a bit of privilege to do.

So for me, I was able to apply for several postdoc grants and failed to get them until there was finally one that I succeeded in getting.

I was in a position to do that because my institute was happy to pay me for another year after I finished my PhD, and my supervisor was happy to keep me around in the lab, and my visa status didn’t depend on me securing funding right away.

So, and I didn’t have family to take care of at that time.

So it’s really like a lot of privileges came together that allowed me to even fail that much.

And that’s also something we need to think about. Who gets to fail? And then who gets to talk about failure.

I always had this kind of secret plan B, which was to open a cinema.

And I think a lot of my friends in science, if you ask them, they always have like a secret plan B. And it’s usually to do with doing something lovely like opening a bakery or opening a bike shop.

And for me it was opening a cinema, a small indie cinema.

I don’t know if I would have done it actually if I left science. But it was kind of a nice fantasy to escape to, and it sometimes still is.

But I still think, "Oh, I can open a cinema if if everything else fails."

But I would not think of it as a failure.

Because I think there’s a lot of ways to leave science, or to leave academia, and do really interesting and really cool things.

So a lot of my friends who were at university with me are not practicing scientists anymore. Or at least not research scientists, but they do really cool things in industry, in education, in all kinds of sectors.

So this view of leaving science as a failure, I think, is quite problematic as well.

I think it’s really important to share failures as well, in order to distinguish what is a personal failure and what is a system failing you.

And if I submit a grant application and I don’t get the grant, that’s fine.

That might be that my idea wasn’t good enough. Or the grant wasn’t well enough thought out.

But if 100 of my friends submit grant applications and then only 10 of them, only five of them, get a grant, then that maybe points to there being not enough money for research or not enough funding.

And I think we need to open up about failures as well to see where there are places in the system where the system actually could be improved.

#739. <i>The Selfish Gene</i>, 50 years on — it’s time for an update

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nathaniel Comfort is a historian of science based in Baltimore, Maryland, USA.

Richard Dawkins set out how genes drive evolution in his popular 1976 book. Credit: Greg White/Fairfax Media/Getty

I first read The Selfish Gene in the 1980s, as a graduate student in neurobiology and animal behaviour. I admired the clarity with which biologist Richard Dawkins distilled mid-twentieth-century work in evolutionary biology.

The idea at the core of the book, published in 1976, was thrillingly simple: that a living organism is just a gene’s way of making more organisms that can carry the gene down the generations.

Dawkins’s paradox: dissecting the body’s battle to keep selfish genes in check

Dawkins’s paradox: dissecting the body’s battle to keep selfish genes in check

Back then, The Selfish Gene seemed pretty harmless. Dawkins’s ideas tracked with mainstream sociobiology. It was a popular book that covered exactly the sort of ideas that my lecturers were already teaching.

Re-reading it now, with decades of scholarship in the history of biology under my belt, it seems less benign. The determinism baked into the “gene’s-eye view” in the book troubles me, as does the passivity of the organism in Dawkins’s telling — a “vehicle”, a mere “replicator”. The implication: that traits such as aggression are hard-wired into people. Fortunately, over the past couple of decades, new tools, fresh models and scholars in many disciplines have begun to embrace the complex reality of biology. Readers in search of an understanding of life on Earth today would do better to reach for books that take a broader view.

The Selfish Gene was the apotheosis of the ‘modern evolutionary synthesis’. That theory uses mathematics to quantify species evolution at the population level, through changes in the frequency of different versions of genes, known as alleles, across time and space.

Dawkins wrote in The Selfish Gene that the gene’s-eye view was “implicit” in the 1930s writings of modern-synthesis pioneer (and eugenicist) Ronald Fisher and his contemporaries, but was made “explicit” by evolutionary biologists George Williams and William Hamilton, in the 1960s. “For me,” he wrote, “their insight had a visionary quality. But I found their expressions of it too laconic, not full-throated enough.” The Selfish Gene, then, takes the ideas to their extreme.

Richard Dawkins book of the dead is haunted by ghosts of past works

Richard Dawkins book of the dead is haunted by ghosts of past works

The modern synthesis blends two branches of evolutionary biology and genetics: neo-Darwinian evolution and Mendelian genetics. Neo-Darwinian evolution was established in the 1890s by biologist August Weismann in his book Die Keimplasma (The Germ Plasm). The book builds off On the Origin of Species, in which Charles Darwin outlines a central tenet — organisms evolve over many generations through an internal process called natural selection. This is the Darwinism of the first edition of On the Origin of Species, published in 1859. Yet over five successive editions, published between then and 1872, Darwin had given increasing credence to the ‘effects of use and disuse’ — the idea, associated with naturalist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, that characteristics acquired during an organism’s lifetime can be inherited. Darwin wrote, for example, about blind cave fish (Astyanax mexicanus). Their ancestors had eyes when they first nosed into a lightless cave. But after going unused for generations, the eyes degenerated, and the change gradually became heritable.

Darwin saw no reason that his theories couldn’t accommodate such phenomena. He didn’t speculate on mechanisms. Today, an evolutionary biologist might argue that any animal that put less energy than its neighbours into making a complex but useless structure, such as an unused eye, would have surplus energy to devote to, say, bigger gonads or defending its territory, and thus would gain a survival advantage. To Weismann, however, incorporating use and disuse into Darwinism was a dangerous move towards teleology, and risked ceding biological change to bishops and mystics. He proposed that only the germ plasm (the material carried in sperm and egg cells) was passed from parents to offspring. Nothing outside could affect what was transmitted.

Trays containing the entire human genome, split into more than 20,000 fragments of DNA.Credit: James King-Holmes/SPL

The second field that makes up the modern synthesis, Mendelian genetics, was invented not by Gregor Mendel, the nineteenth-century monk after whom the field is named, but by naturalist William Bateson, in his strange and brilliant 1902 book, Mendel’s Principles of Heredity: A Defence. Mendel ran experiments crossing peas, and in 1866 published a paper describing rules that governed how traits were passed down — how many offspring of a green and yellow pea cross would be green and how many yellow, for instance. We now know that only some traits, controlled by single genes, follow the simplistic patterns he observed.

The conservative Mendel claimed only to have found a law “valid for Pisum” (the pea genus); Bateson claimed that all heredity followed Mendel’s laws. Bateson’s book was ‘a defence’ against the theories of his rival and erstwhile best friend, Walter Weldon, who argued that such neat, simple laws do not describe how nature works. Weldon pointed out that traits such as height vary continuously, in a bell-shaped, normal distribution. He argued that such traits result from many factors, both hereditary and environmental.

In the end, as historian Gregory Radick has argued, Mendelism became the universally accepted form of heredity more for practical reasons than because it captured an essential truth. It’s easy to teach and methodologically simple.

Both components of the modern synthesis focus on the gene as the sole determinant of heredity. Both halves reached essentially universal acceptance well before Dawkins came along — the spit and swagger of the field’s proponents keeping challenges and alternatives at bay.

To a historian, this universal acceptance sounds close to ideology. Fortunately, since The Selfish Gene was published, scientists’ understanding of the basic mechanisms that drive evolution has changed drastically.

#736. Thousands of German gamblers could sue for their money back

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

German gamblers may finally be able to beat the house, thanks to new court rulings in the EU and in Germany. The decisions could help gambling addicts — but the legal road might be difficult.

A German court has followed the European Court of Justice in finding that gamblers can seek compensation from gambling companies if they lost money when online casinos and fruit machines were illegal in Germany.

The verdicts could have major consequences for gambling addicts, as thousands of people could potentially bring civil lawsuits against gambling companies.

A series of court decisions at regional, federal, and European level have found in favor of gamblers in the last year, beginning with the Higher Regional Court Stuttgart in September 2025, which agreed with a plaintiff in the state of Baden-Württemberg who sued the Malta-based online betting company Tipico Games.

The plaintiff lost around €10,000 ($11,200) between 2020 and 2022, but because online gambling was prohibited in Germany until 2021, the court found that operators had therefore received the winnings without legal basis and must return them.

Tipico Games then appealed to the Federal Court of Justice (BGH), the highest civil and criminal court in Germany. In an initial verbal hearing in mid-September this year, the court followed the principle of the plaintiffs' case on one key point: That gamblers have the right to claim back losses if the companies did not have a license in Germany at the time the losses were incurred. But a final decision on the case is only expected to be made in January 2027.

Online casinos and fruit machines were banned in Germany from 2008 to 2021, but several gambling operators were active in the country because they had gaming licenses in other EU countries.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In April this year, the European Court of Justice ruled that EU law does not preclude a member state from "prohibiting certain services," or from "attaching civil-law consequences to that prohibition." In other words, even if a gambling company has a legitimate license in one member state, that doesn't override national gambling laws elsewhere.

Thomas Dünchheim, a business lawyer at global law firm Greenberg Traurig who specializes in gambling law, said law firms were now gathering clients — sometimes trawling the internet with the help of AI tools — to prepare massive collective lawsuits. Dünchheim himself has people who have lost tens of thousands of euros come to him seeking representation.

"The pendulum is swinging more and more towards the consumer. It's a bit like in America — we're seeing a mass phenomenon like the Dieselgate lawsuits against VW," he told DW. "And there are lawyers who will collect all these little cases, bundle them, and then maybe even drive it forward with the help of a legal financing firm. It's a good business for all involved, and the ones that will have to pay are the gambling firms who operated unlawful gambling in Germany."

The decisions could bring a measure of help for addicts, as online gambling can be particularly dangerous for people with addiction issues. According to Tobias Hayer, a psychologist at the Institute for Public Health and Nursing Research at Bremen University, that comes down to four main features of online gambling: Anonymity and the consequent lack of social control, 24/7 accessibility, the frictionless nature of cashless transactions, and the high frequency of games played.

"These court verdicts are not surprising at all," Hayer told DW, but he added that he had an ambivalent attitude to them. "On the one hand I can imagine that this will be a huge relief to many gamblers who had an addiction problem. On the other hand, if these people suddenly get a lot of money in their hands, but they haven't worked through their problems, then of course there's a danger of recidivism."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But Dünchheim suggested that the gamblers may not have such an easy ride when making their claims. It's true that German law has now concluded that if the gambling contract that the player makes with the company turns out to be unlawful in the country where they live, the player can claim their losses back. But only if the player themselves "did not act illegally," as Dünchheim put it.

"You also have to say: Many of these players deliberately went to games in this gray zone because the winnings are potentially bigger," he said. "Because the companies don't pay taxes."

"Then the defense team of the gambling company will of course say: 'You took part in an illegal game yourself, so you were acting illegally.' And this question of interpretation is not simple," he added. "It's a very interesting intellectual question, but it's also existential for the gambling companies."

The Tipico case is perhaps particularly interesting in the German context because, although the company is based in Malta, it was founded in 2004 by a group of German lawyers. The company is a big employer, with several thousand employees worldwide, and has been a sponsor of more than one top German football club. Tipico has also said that it has rigorous consumer protection measures in place to identify and prevent dangerous betting behavior.

But there was some legal ambiguity about its online operations in Germany up until 2021.

"They always had lawyers who could attest that what they are doing conforms to European law, because it is permitted in a European Union member state," said Dünchheim. "But that is a false assumption, as it has now been established that a gambling permit in another EU state doesn't apply in Germany, because unlike other areas, gambling law isn't harmonized across the bloc."

"Tipico was started by two businessmen and grew big in a gray zone," as Dünchheim put it. "They had professional lobbying firms on board and they hired experienced lawyers, they had private equity firms on board. But of course they are carrying a huge financial risk."
