#727. AI-assisted dying? Doris Dörrie's new film addresses prospect of care robots

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

While the world debates the dangers of artificial intelligence, filmmaker Doris Dörrie explores how humanoid robots could change the way we deal with aging, caregiving and how people choose to die.

Hamburg in the near future: Instead of human drivers, robots deliver parcels. In cafes, robots roll between the tables, serving diners. On the streets, one encounters humanoid robots walking dogs — or the other way around, people taking their robot dogs for a walk.

This is the setting of Doris Dörrie's new film, "Frau Winkler verlässt das Haus" ("Mrs. Winkler Leaves the House"). At the core of the plot is an elderly woman who can no longer live on her own after a fall. With her only daughter unable to provide permanent care, the solution seems simple enough: a care robot with a built-in EOL program, or "End of Life" mode. This robot not only assists with everyday life but can also provide assisted dying under certain conditions, namely when the person explicitly wishes to end their life and meets the relevant medical criteria.

Dörrie's film tackles several major social issues with remarkable lightness. These include the challenges facing aging societies such as Germany, Japan and China, the question of dying on one's own terms and a mother-daughter relationship that raises questions of guilt and responsibility. Even though the story is set in Germany, such issues resonate globally.

"I write about what personally moves and interests me," Dörrie told DW.

One of the best-known contemporary German film directors, Dörrie achieved her breakthrough in 1985 with the comedy "Men…" She gained further international recognition with films such as 2008's "Cherry Blossoms" and "Greetings from Fukushima" (2016).

Assisted suicide is one of the most complex ethical questions of our time. Laws vary around the world. Though some countries permit active euthanasia under certain conditions, others prohibit and criminalize all forms of assisted dying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In her film, Dörrie asks what happens when artificial intelligence begins calculating the cost of caring for an elderly person and weighing whether that cost is still "worth" bearing for society.

The underlying idea isn't new, Dörrie said, pointing to the Japanese legend of Narayama, which is also mentioned in the film. According to the legend, the eldest children were responsible for taking their ageing parents to a mountain and leaving them there to die because there was not enough food for everyone. "And that's also the debate we are currently facing to a certain extent: Can we really afford to let older people live longer and longer?"

In Dörrie's film, elderly people are allowed to make their own decisions once they reach a certain state of health — but they can't change their minds afterwards. Yet what does it really mean to make a decision freely? "It's a tricky situation," says Dörrie, because the question is to what extent one is also pressured into making this decision, "not only because it makes more economic sense, but also because one is no longer a burden on one's loved ones — in this case, one's daughter..."

The film often raises these questions indirectly and with plenty of dark humor. At one point, a care adviser presents the EOL feature to Mrs. Winkler as an attractive and, above all, straightforward additional option, making it sound as though there would be nothing more for her to worry about.

Dörrie is not interested in demonizing AI in her film — quite the opposite. In the film, the care robot, which Mrs. Winkler names Pavlovich, helps the elderly woman rediscover some of her zest for life and get out of the house.

"When you travel through Germany, you see small houses everywhere, and statistics show that an elderly person lives alone in every other house," Dörrie said. "If AI can help in these circumstances, why not use it?" She said she sought to explore this ambiguity in her film. Dividing things into black and white would neither be interesting nor, in her view, accurate.

Dörrie and her crew were surprised during filming by how quickly people can develop emotional bonds with robots. She attributes this to the human brain. "We regard anything that moves and speaks as a living being. We can't help it," she explains. And that is precisely what we need to pay attention to when interacting with AI, Dörrie says. "How often are we truly aware that we are talking to a machine rather than a living being? These are things we still have to learn."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As AI develops, it seems that the boundaries between humans and machines are becoming increasingly blurred. That is precisely why we need to talk about it, Doris Dörrie says. In her view, things become problematic "when we can no longer distance ourselves from technology and stop forming our own thoughts."

Human beings need to ask who we are and what truly defines us, Dörrie said. "I believe there is a major difference between robots and us, and that is the ability to play. A robot might be able to initiate a game, she explains, "but play itself is something profoundly human because it has no particular meaning or purpose."

Alongside these philosophical questions about what it means to be human, Dörrie makes a clear call for AI regulation. "At some point, we had to discuss nuclear weapons internationally, too. We've talked about all kinds of issues in the past, and we haven't just talked about them — we've also managed to find solutions," she points out.

"And I believe we need to move very quickly on this, too," Dörrie said.

#699. EU promotes sovereign, trusted AI as it struggles to catch US and China

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

At an international AI summit in Dublin, EU leaders promoted trusted and independent artificial intelligence. Critics question whether the bloc can close the gap with the US and China while maintaining strict regulation.

If supremacy in artificial intelligence was an Olympic discipline, there would only be two serious contenders for gold on current trajectories: the US and China. The European Union, as has been the case in many areas of cutting-edge technology in recent times, is barely in the AI conversation.

Former European Central Bank President Mario Draghi, whose 2024 report highlighted the EU's desperate need to be more innovative to become more competitive, said recently that AI is "perhaps the most promising" route the EU has to raise growth today. However, he decried the fact that the European Union controls little of the value chain.

"Being cut off from AI, once the economy runs on it, would be more like being cut off from the US financial system," he wrote in an opinion piece for the Financial Times. "The effects would be catastrophic."

Draghi's spirit was on full display in Dublin on Wednesday at an international AI summit the Irish government convened as part of its six-month stint hosting the rotating EU presidency.

The summit's motto, "Harnessing AI to Revolutionize Europe's Competitiveness," might as well have been dreamed up by the Italian former prime minister.

Harnessing AI has become a lot more complicated. A slew of controversies around AI agents going rogue, from the Hugging Face attack in June when 1,200 agents hacked an online platform, to an Anthropic-designed agent sending a fake tip to US police over an unsolved murder, have caused alarm.

Many from within the tech industry, including Microsoft founder Bill Gates and the leading AI frontier labs themselves, have called for a development pausein order for safety measures to catch up.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet positivity was largely the name of the game at the summit, with tech and AI industry leaders joining Irish and EU politicians to declare AI's transformative economic and societal potential — while also emphasizing the need for strong regulation and safety standards.

Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin made it clear that Ireland was all in on AI. He echoed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's recent assertion that the technology represented a "tipping point." He also repeatedly highlighted what he sees as the bloc's commitment to safety.

"We are determined to capture the dividend by mitigating the risks," Martin told the event. "In Europe, we have charted our path ... balancing innovation and opportunity with a trustworthy, human-centered approach to AI."

Meanwhile, Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, security and democracy, revealed at the event that the EU had begun its first enforcement actions under its new AI Act, requesting information around security and safety from advanced AI model providers.

However, other topics that concern AI's many critics, from those fearing the massive environmental impact of data centers to others warning about possible AI-related job losses, were largely absent from the discussions.

Outside the venue, a group of protesters led by People Before Profit, a left-wing Irish political party, criticized the summit for not focusing on these issues.

"There is a deliberate blurring of the line here with the type of AI that is being promoted," Alexandra Day, one of the protest organizers, told DW.

"It is really being pushed on workers with very little consent. There's no right for workers to opt out of using AI now that it's coming into the workplace."

A sense of urgency was palpable from the speakers inside the summit. Executives from some of the world's biggest AI and tech firms talked up Europe's potential. Yet the EU evidently has plenty of ground to catch up on in terms of AI development.

Despite ramping up its data center capacity, it still lags far behind the US and China. It hosts 5% of the world's AI computing capacity compared to around 75% for the US.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The EU is conspicuously absent from lists of the leading AI frontier labs, with only French company Mistral coming close to rivaling the top labs. Its production of leading-edge chips is also nowhere near that of the top US or Taiwanese producers.

As part of its plan to make ground on the US and China, the Irish government, in its role as EU presidency host, presented a policy document at the event.

The so-called "Dublin Declaration" outlines political commitments to strengthen Europe's AI capabilities, including infrastructure investment and financial backing for European AI companies.

In keeping with Draghi's calls for Europe to develop its own AI sovereignty, particularly in supply chains and infrastructure, the declaration suggests that European firms reliant on non-EU cloud and computing services may face additional compliance pressures.

However, not everyone is convinced by the EU's capacity to either ramp up AI capacity or develop effective regulation.

Eddie Wilson, CEO of European airline Ryanair, said he doubted Brussels could regulate AI well without stifling innovation.

"The last thing you want is people regulating this industry who don't know anything about it," he told DW. "That's generally what happens in Brussels."

Ryanair recently made a major deal with Google to use its cloud data system and its AI platform Gemini Enterprise. It's precisely the kind of collaboration with US AI supply chains that the EU says it wants companies to move away from.

"I worry for Europe because these tech companies need to move at speed," said Wilson. He believes the environment in the US is more amenable to innovation.

"If they're not going to do it here, they're going to do it elsewhere. They're going to do it in China and they're going to do it in the US."

#687. Can science make your dog live longer? Longevity craze comes to pets

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

Not just for humans: gene therapy to extend longevity is under investigation for dogs, too.Credit: Juliana Yamada/Los Angeles Times/Getty

Vera Gorbunova has attended many a longevity conference over her decades of studying ageing. But never one quite like this.

Earlier this month, Gorbunova, a researcher at Rochester University in New York, joined scientists from industry and academia — and a fair few of their dogs — for the Animal Longevity Summit in Toronto, Canada. Given it was the inaugural summit, it was small. But it highlighted a growing interest in the science of extending the lifespan of pets.

On the agenda were presentations by academic researchers such as Gorbunova, who studies ageing in various animal species. Others presented projects about understanding cancer in dogs, regeneration in axolotls and the genetics of mammals that thrive in extreme environments. Alongside the university scientists were researchers at companies pursuing gene therapies for dogs, probiotic kibble for cats and cryopreservation of pets.

Big dogs age faster than little ones — rogue ‘jumping genes’ might be to blame

Big dogs age faster than little ones — rogue ‘jumping genes’ might be to blame

“It was maybe a somewhat different crowd of people than you see at the typical ageing conferences,” Gorbunova says.

The conference reflected a market reality: as the pursuit of increasing human longevity and healthspan has grown, fuelled by hefty investment, it only stands to reason that some of that interest would spill over to pets, says Cameron Hurlburt, a senior analyst at Ani VC, a venture-capital firm in Miami, Florida. The US pet- and animal-health market is estimated to be worth US$150 billion and could grow as more people in the United States purchase pet health insurance, he says.

Most of the current efforts to promote longer pet healthspans focus on improving animal diets, for example with probiotic food formulations, Hurlburt says. And when it comes to therapies, many companies are looking to repurpose drugs that are already approved for humans, rather than starting from scratch.

But not everyone is taking that approach. The Cat Health Company in Bucharest presented its strategy for identifying new drugs for ageing-associated diseases in cats, including a muscle-wasting condition called sarcopenia, and kidney disease. The company has two compounds in clinical trials now, with others on the way, says Alex Băciţa, co-founder and chief operating officer of the company.

How ageing changes our genes — huge epigenetic atlas gives clearest picture yet

How ageing changes our genes — huge epigenetic atlas gives clearest picture yet

Others are venturing into gene therapies. Rejuvenate Bio, a biotechnology company in San Diego, California, is working on one to treat mitral valve disease, the most common heart condition in dogs. But co-founder and chief scientific officer Noah Davidsohn hopes that this will be just the first use for the therapy, and that the same treatment will eventually be used to treat metabolic syndromes and improve longevity. Rejuvenate has worked to decrease the cost of manufacturing gene therapies, which are complex treatments, to a level that would be compatible with the pet market.

Another company, called Genflow Biosciences, is pursuing a gene therapy to enhance longevity and reduce sarcopenia in dogs. If the drug shows success, the company hopes to sell it to a larger animal-health company, and then use the proceeds to help to fund studies of the same approach in humans, says Eric Leire, founder and chief executive of the firm in Brussels.

Academic researchers also stand to gain by interacting with the latest companies to spring up, said Noah Snyder-Mackler, a comparative geroscientist at Arizona State University in Tempe, before the meeting. Government grants for studying dogs often focus on applying the results to human health, rather than canine health. That means that academic researchers might need to collaborate with industry to conduct studies that lead to treatments for dogs.

“We don’t have the resources to follow up with dog-centric interventions,” says Snyder-Mackler, a researcher on the Dog Aging Project, a large collaboration to study ageing in pooches. Gorbunova says she enjoyed the meeting. “It was a revelation to me to see how interested people are in extending the life of their pets,” she says.

#672. China's influence in the gaming industry is growing

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Home to more than 700 million gamers, China is the world's largest gaming market — but it's also one of the most tightly regulated. The effects reach far beyond China, impacting players around the world.

In a dark underground hideout, dim light spills from a handful of oil lamps. A comrade fiddles with a rifle. A red flag hangs on one of the roughly hewn stone walls, bearing a hammer and sickle on a white star — the symbol of the ChineseWorkers' and Peasants' Red Army. Weapons are scattered on the ground. One is picked up, and soon the action moves into the snowy forest, where gunfire erupts among the trees.

Such a scene could fit in a new installment of "Call of Duty," the popular first-person shooter game that transports players to battlefields past, present, and future. But it is actually from "The Defiant." The game is currently being developed by the Chinese studio Hoothanes Technology in Hangzhou. It tells the story of Chinese forces fending off the Japanese army in the 1930s and 1940s.

Developer Connor Xu tells DW the weapons featured in the game are unique. They were used only in Asia and are therefore unfamiliar to many Western players, he says. The same goes for the story, which Xu says has never before been told in a video game.

"The Defiant" is also designed to appeal to an international audience. In just a few years, China has emerged as a major player in the global gaming industry despite strict regulations, censorship and a former ban on video game consoles.

More than 700 million people in China regularly play video games. According to market research company Newzoo, most consider gaming an important part of their lives. Many use games to stay in touch with friends.

"Games make life more interesting," developer Xu says. "I can try different roles, different stories, different characters, because we only have one life to live, but we can play a role in another story. That's really attractive, I think, to Chinese users."

People in China primarily play games on PCs and smartphones, while consoles are much less common. There are historical reasons for that: While gamers in Europe and North America debated whether PlayStation or Xbox was the better console in the early 2000s, the devices were not officially sold in China between 2000 and 2014. Chinese authorities said the restrictions were intended to protect children and teenagers from becoming addicted to gaming.

Minors in China are currently allowed to play online games for no more than three hours a week. There are no such limits for adults, but gaming is subject to strict controls. Anyone who wants to play must register using their real name and a personal identification number. That effectively allows the state to track who plays what and when, as well as whom they communicate with.

There is also a gray area that the Chinese government appears to tolerate. Some players log in using VPNs, giving them access to games that are not officially available in China. Some younger players use their parents' accounts to get around the limits on gaming time.

Despite its strict controls on underage gamers, China has become increasingly receptive to video games in general, having recognized the industry's enormous economic potential. Early on, games released for Chinese players often appeared to be copies of Western titles. At the same time, Chinese tech companies such as Tencent and NetEase invested in numerous Western gaming companies.

One distinctive feature of the Chinese market is its licensing system. "Unlike a lot of the other big video games markets in the world, China has a tightly regulated and licensed official video games market," George E. Osborn tells DW. The journalist advises NGOs and governments on video games and spoke at the Gamescom congress. In his book "Power Play," he describes how authoritarian states use video games to pursue political objectives.

The rule for all games in China is simple: No license, no sales. "That system essentially forces developers who want to release their video games to go through multiple layers of approval from China's Ministry of Propaganda, Ministry of Culture," Osborn says.

Games are prohibited from containing material that threatens China's unity, sovereignty or territorial integrity, among other restrictions. Pornographic content and gambling are also banned. Games may not incite crimes that threaten national security or spread information authorities believe could disrupt public order.

"The whole point around this criteria is that it's deliberately designed to be pretty vague," Osborn says. Whether a game violates the rules is a matter of interpretation. Sometimes games are altered even after release. In the 2025 action role-playing game "Wuchang: Fallen Feathers," for example, enemies based on famous Chinese figures from the Ming Dynasty suddenly could no longer be killed. Instead, they would collapse from exhaustion.

The Chinese action role-playing game "Black Myth: Wukong" became an unexpected international hit in 2024. By then, it was clear Chinese developers could do more than cater to the domestic market — they could create successful games for a global audience as well. The game was inspired by the 16th-century Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West."

Osborn sees nothing wrong with bringing Chinese culture to audiences around the world. The question, he says, is how much the state actually intervenes in the games themselves. "I think in general, video game players are actually quite deeply skeptical of these kinds of things. They are generally very good at spotting when someone might be selling to them or someone might be propagandizing. And so I think if it's too obvious, it won't work," he says.

Because of the licensing system, Western developers also have to comply with government requirements if they want to sell their games in China. And they do want to, Osborn says, because the market is too big to ignore. "But I think when you start thinking about the potential impact this has on creative standards around the world, I think it's really important that developers ask themselves the question of what will we or won't we compromise on here?"

He fears the real danger lies in self-censorship. That could lead developers, for example, to leave queer characters out of their games. That would represent a major step backward, he says, because games help many people explore their identities.

China is not the only country where games are modified to comply with national regulations. In Germany, for example, symbols that violate the country's constitution, such as the swastika, may not be shown in games unless the game in question explicitly contributes to the country's culture of remembrance. Depictions of extreme violence also have to be removed from German versions.

Glorifying violence is prohibited in China, too, yet Xu's team is still allowed to develop a war game. How does this add up? Xu explains it this way: "I think in this game, the most important thing is not violence. The most important thing is to tell history."

Xu says the team is committed to delivering a historically accurate product. Whether it succeeds will be for historians to judge.

#666. Are salaries getting worse? Many scientists think so

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Linda Nordling is a freelance journalist in Cape Town, South Africa.

This article is the second in a series discussing the results of Nature’s 2026 science-job satisfaction survey. It’s the latest edition of such surveys, which started in 2010; the last two took place in 2018 and 2021. The 2026 survey, created in partnership with Thinks Insight & Strategy, a research consultancy in London, launched in May and was advertised on nature.com, in Springer Nature digital products and through e-mail campaigns. It had 3,882 self-selecting respondents across 133 countries with 31% describing themselves as female and 19% as belonging to a minority ethnic group in their country of work. The full survey data sets are available at go.nature.com/4b2drrc.

Umar, a mathematics lecturer in northern Nigeria, has worked at his university for more than ten years. In that time, he’s had only one pay rise: in 2024, when the government raised the national minimum wage. With no inflation- or promotion-based adjustments, his income no longer covers his basic living costs. Instead, he has to borrow money, take on extra jobs and cut back on essential spending. “Unfortunately, my experience is not an isolated one” for Nigerian scientists, he says.

On the other side of the Atlantic Ocean, Ashley — an early-career physicist employed on a fixed-term contract in a university in the eastern United States — says she is much worse off than her parents, neither of whom have degrees. “It’s really messed up that I have a job that requires a PhD in science, yet I’m paid US$20,000 less per year than my father earned at his job 20 years ago, before accounting for inflation.” Ashley lists the things she can’t afford, including children (her pay won’t cover childcare, nor putting them through university) and home ownership. She thinks she did everything ‘right’ — for example, having jobs alongside her undergraduate studies to avoid debt. “Yet I am still locked out of the middle-class existence I have worked myself half to death for,” she says, adding: “It sucks. It really, really sucks.”

Umar and Ashley (not their real names) live in countries with vastly different resources for research and costs of living. But their stories reflect a global theme. When Nature’s careers team surveyed them and nearly 4,000 other scientists earlier this year about their salaries, less than half said they had received a pay rise in the past 12 months. Around one-third said that their salaries covered only basic expenses, and one in ten said their income failed to do even that.

The survey asked respondents to convert their gross (before-taxes) salary into US dollars, then choose the range into which it falls. More than half earn less than US$50,000 a year, and 22% make at least $80,000. In 2021, when Nature last ran this survey, 38% earned below $50,000 and 32% earned $80,000 or more. But this apparent drop in global salaries might be because of geographical shifts in those surveyed — particularly a rise in respondents from Asia, who made up 10% in 2021 and 39% this year. From continents with enough respondents for comparison, North American scientists earn the most, followed by those in Europe, then Asia (see ‘The scientist’s wallet’).

Industry salaries exceed those in academia by 66%, and more scientists in industry are satisfied with their salary (58%) than are those in academia (43%). But even in the private sector, some think that they should earn more. “It feels like I’m making less and less every year,” says a researcher working at a biomedical technology company in a large city in the midwestern United States, who, like many scientists Nature spoke to, asked to remain anonymous when discussing pay concerns.

She moved from working at a university to her current job four years ago after discovering that she was pregnant, because she judged childcare expenses to be unaffordable on her previous salary. But despite having a dozen years of work experience in both industry and academia, she says that she is still paid like a recent graduate.

“I love science and what I do, but I also feel undervalued,” she says.

Scientists in the United States earn the most out of the ten countries in the survey that had more than 100 respondents, which means the results from these nations can be compared sensibly. Some 65% of United States-based scientists report earning more than $80,000 a year. The lowest wages are found in India, where 53% earn less than $15,000 a year. Comparing continents, the lowest salaries are found in Africa, where 61% earn below $15,000 per year.

We need to talk about salaries in science

We need to talk about salaries in science

However, the survey’s self-reported salary figures in converted US dollars do not reflect what those incomes can buy on the ground. A dollar buys more in India than in the United States: nearly five times more. According to purchasing-power calculations by the International Monetary Fund, a $15,000 salary in India is comparable to a $70,000 salary in the United States. When adjusted for purchasing power, average salaries in the survey for Canada overtake those in the United States, salaries in Germany come close to US ones and the wide salary gaps between emerging economies and wealthier nations shrink. And it’s important to note that a nation’s average salary in the survey can be skewed by sample biases with respect to factors such as location within a nation, employment sector and career stage.

In Brazil, where 21% of respondents report earning less than $15,000, a low or modest salary by US or western-European standards can “provide a reasonably comfortable life locally”, especially outside the most expensive cities such as Rio de Janeiro or Sao Paolo, says Haroldo Ribeiro, a physicist at the State University of Maringá in Brazil. “Still, I would not conclude that Brazilian scientists are generally well paid,” he says. Although salaries in public universities there have increased in the past few years, this comes after a long period of stagnation, he says, making it a recovery, not a raise.

Only 44% of people in the total sample are satisfied with their pay, but this varies between countries. Significantly more scientists in Canada (61%), Germany (68%) and the United States (55%) are satisfied with their income than the global average. The countries with at least 100 respondents that had the lowest numbers of scientists satisfied with their salary are Turkey (27%), China (39%) and Italy (40%).

China’s lower-than-average satisfaction with salary comes despite survey data suggesting that Chinese salaries have risen in US-dollar terms since Nature asked scientists the same question in 2021. Some 11% of Chinese respondents reported earning more than $80,000 this year, nearly doubling from 6% in 2021. Over the same time, in the United Kingdom, the proportion earning more than $80,000 grew from 19% to only 22%.

Salaries can vary substantially between China’s economically developed coastal areas, and its more-sparsely populated west, as well as between universities, says survey respondent Jingrui Sun, a freshwater ecologist at Yunnan University in Kunming, China. He describes his salary as “sufficient for me to live comfortably”, and says that it is common for research-intensive universities and institutions in wealthy parts of the country to offer employees performance-related pay, as well as housing subsidies and laboratory start-up packages.

But good salaries in China come with extra demands, Sun says. “Part of the package is linked to periodic assessments, and if the required targets are not met, remuneration in the following period can be reduced substantially.” He says a few of his colleagues have had their pay docked this year, after their university introduced more-stringent assessment criteria. “Such changes can have real consequences for staff retention, and have prompted academics to leave and take positions at other institutions,” he says.

Annual pay rises are not the global norm, the survey shows. Only 45% of respondents say they had received a raise in the previous 12 months, and 6% report a cut in pay. Industry researchers are more likely than the average result to have had a pay rise (54%), whereas the opposite is true for those who earn less than $50,000 a year (42% of whom received one).

Many survey-takers are frustrated that they aren’t getting paid more. One non-tenure-track US researcher who works in a biology department says that she exceeds her department’s tenure criteria and outperforms several of her tenure-track colleagues. Those colleagues are paid at least $20,000 more than her annually and get more research funding. “Yet my department chairs keep looking me dead in the eye and saying there’s no appetite for raises” for people like her, she says.

What’s the secret sauce for happy scientists at work? These eight countries offer some clues

What’s the secret sauce for happy scientists at work? These eight countries offer some clues

When salaries grow, it’s often not enough. One researcher with a fixed-term contract in Pune, India, says his public-sector salary has not kept up with “skyrocketing urban inflation” in the city of seven million people. He says that rent, public transport and groceries consume most of his pay. “At this salary, no one can even think of home or car loans,” he says. Add a child, he says, and “it’s just a matter of survival”.

In Europe, where 27% of respondents report earning more than $80,000 a year, salaries vary massively between countries, says Norbert Bencze, president of Eurodoc, an organization for early-career researchers in Europe. “A good salary in the Netherlands is something very different from a good salary in Poland or Hungary.” However, living costs outpacing pay increases are a common problem across the continent, he says. “Some researchers have seen their actual purchasing power fall quite radically, in some cases cut in half over the past ten years, even though they got regular pay rises.” Although Nature’s salary survey was of post-PhD researchers and lab technicians, Eurodoc’s survey of doctoral pay in 2025 showed that PhD students earned below minimum wage in five European countries: Hungary, Ireland, Poland, Romania and Ukraine (see go.nature.com/4s7m1tu).

Fairer, more transparent salary-setting would be welcome, even if scientists’ wages continue to underwhelm, survey participants say. “It is not only about paying more, but about making compensation feel clear, consistent and linked to contribution,” says a materials scientist in India. People should understand how salaries are decided, what the path to a raise or promotion looks like and whether their pay is competitive with the market, he says.

Researchers who had not taken the survey felt similarly when Nature spoke to them about the results. In Portugal, academic salaries have risen in recent years, mainly to keep up with inflation, says Ronaldo Sousa, an aquatic ecologist at the Interdisciplinary Centre of Marine and Environmental Research near Porto. However, to get a pay rise that is substantially above inflation, scientists must move up the academic ladder, for example from assistant professor to associate professor. “We might publish a dozen high-impact papers in a year, but this will not necessarily result in any increase in salary,” he says.

#649. How reliant is Ukraine on the US-controlled Starlink internet service?

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Kyiv keeps issuing warnings that the satellite internet system Starlink is being restricted in Ukraine. How dependent is the country on the system, and what would happen if it went down?

Few technological systems have played such an important role in the war in Ukraine as Starlink, central to the communications, reconnaissance and drone operations of the Ukrainian armed forces. There are currently widespread concerns that Elon Musk's satellite internet service in Ukraine may be restricted or even switched off. In recent days, Kyiv has repeatedly reported disruptions and restrictions affecting its use.

Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine has made extensive use of the satellite internet service, which is operated by the US company SpaceX. With it, military personell can continue to communicate and exchange data, even when infrastructure has been destroyed or cellphone networks are down.

According to the Center for Security Studies (CSS) at ETH Zurich, around 50,000 Starlink terminals were in use in Ukraine in 2025. These are the system's specialised receiving and transmitting devices, which enable communications on the battlefield. They are also used to relay orders between command levels and receive drone footage.

The importance of the Starlink network can in part be explained by events at the beginning of the war. According to a CSS analysis, the KA-SAT satellite system previously favored by Ukraine was targeted in a cyberattack just hours before Russia's invasion. Starlink quickly became a vital alternative.

When discussing current affairs, the terms "Starlink" and "Starshield" are often used interchangeably.

However, Starlink is SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, whereas Starshield is specifically designed for governmental and military use. While based on the same technological infrastructure, it is designed for security and defense applications.

This distinction matters, because the latest reports of restrictions seem to primarily concern systems used for military purposes. Elon Musk recently stated that Starshield systems are controlled by the US government, whereas Starlink is a commercial service operated by SpaceX.

Alongside communications, Starlink is mainly used for drone operations. The system provides an internet connection for ground, naval and aerial drones.

This connection means video footage can be transmitted almost in real time, while drones can be controlled over long distances. Ukraine uses these systems for reconnaissance and attacks deep behind enemy lines.

According to ETH Zurich, images and GPS coordinates of Russian positions are also transmitted via these communication channels. The data is sent to artillery units and used to coordinate operations.

According to Ukrainian media reports, on Tuesday night, SpaceX temporarily introduced a speed restriction for Starlink terminals in Ukraine, limiting terminals in motion to a speed of about 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph).

Such a restriction has direct consequences for fast-moving Ukrainian drones, some of which travel at speeds of up to 300 kilometers per hour (186 mph). If the connection to the drone is lost, live video footage can no longer be transmitted, and the systems can no longer be controlled in real time. The drones effectively have to continue their mission while flying blind.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Restricting or even shutting down a Starlink network would therefore not only make communication more difficult. It would also affect Ukrainian drone operations, and other military activities.

However, Starlink and its military counterpart, Starshield, are only one essential component of Ukraine's defense system. Ukraine also receives reconnaissance data from western partners, including information about Russian air attacks, missile launches, troop movements and anti-aircraft positions, as well as potential routes to avoid them.

This information helps with air defense and offensive operations. Without this intelligence, it would be significantly harder for Ukraine to carry out long-range drone operations against targets in Russian territory.

The two elements are particularly effective when combined. Reconnaissance data provides information about potential targets and routes, while Starlink ensures that this data can be quickly relayed to units.

This is why reports that the US is limiting access to its reconnaissance data are as worrying as the possibility that Starlink might be throttled. Other NATO countries, such as the United Kingdom and France, can also provide reconnaissance data, but not to the extent as the United States.

Europe has several alternatives to Starlink, including Eutelsat/OneWeb. However, their ability to match Starlink's performance in wartime conditions has not yet been tested on a large scale.

The recurrent concern about possible restrictions makes clear that satellite communications have become a central component of Ukrainian defense. And while relying on a single provider simplifies operations, it also shows how dependent modern armed forces have become on private technology companies. Experts say this marks a fundamental change in warfare.

Meanwhile, Ukraine's successful use of Starlink has helped the system to achieve global recognition.

#603. Global climate body fights for survival: why the IPCC must be saved

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The IPCC has survived crises before — it can do so again.Credit: Pavlo Gonchar/SOPA Images/Sipa USA/Alamy

When the most recent meeting of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), held in Addis Ababa, ended earlier this month, its conclusion drew negative media headlines. The United Nations body — the world’s forum for climate scientists — had failed, not for the first time, to agree a timetable for its next comprehensive review of the science of global climate change.

Global emissions slow — but world hurtles towards 2 °C of warming

Global emissions slow — but world hurtles towards 2 °C of warming

Many countries would like the review, known as the Seventh Assessment Report (AR7), to be published in 2028. This would be in time for a UN climate meeting called the Global Stocktake, at which countries assess their progress towards meeting climate pledges. A number of nations, including some European countries and small island states, want the report to be published ahead of the stocktake. This would allow decisions such as adjustments to pledges to be informed by the latest science.

A second, smaller group, including India, Iran, Kenya, Russia and Saudi Arabia, is arguing that 2028 is too soon. They say that some of the poorest countries lack the capacity to participate in the process of reviewing the report before it is published. They also object to the fact that the studies under review are dominated by science from institutions in high-income countries. However, for AR7, the IPCC says 51% of authors and review editors are from developing countries and nations with economies in transition.

Reviewing IPCC assessment reports is a big undertaking. When AR6 was published in 2023, it ran to more than 7,500 pages and received some 200,000 comments from reviewers around the world.

But the IPCC faces an even more serious problem: it is running out of money. For the first time in its history, it might not have the funds to finish an assessment report. The body relies on voluntary donations from governments and other UN agencies, and these have been falling since 2023 (see ‘Lack of trust’). The funds are also used to support scientists from the poorest countries, allowing them to attend meetings. Many of the countries that want to delay the next report have contributed nothing to the IPCC in years, if ever, although Russia is a notable exception. If contributions continue at current levels, by the end of 2028 the IPCC will be left with just 5 million Swiss francs (US$6 million) — the amount needed for an orderly wind-down of the body.

But there is a way forwards. The IPCC needs more than 20 million Swiss francs to stay operational until the end of 2029, and to complete AR7. Nations must consider increasing their contributions immediately. Other donors, including philanthropists and non-governmental organizations, should also approach the IPCC to see how they can help.

There are those who question whether the world still needs the IPCC. They say that there are faster ways to synthesize climate research, and that much is already known about climate change, its impacts and the measures needed to prevent dangerous consequences. Last week, a separate UN report confirmed that countries are not on track to limit global warming to within 1.5 °C of pre-industrial levels.

How to fight climate change without the US: a guide to global action

How to fight climate change without the US: a guide to global action

But these arguments overlook the true value of the IPCC, which includes its processes. IPCC reports are produced in a highly consultative way — scientists from the richest to the poorest countries collaborate, ensuring that voices from around the world are heard. This global, scientist-led process also ensures that the quality of the evidence under review takes precedence over political considerations. Once the scientists agree on the main text, governments are involved in writing the summary report, and can choose whether and how to act on the findings. But they cannot change the main text of the assessment report.

The IPCC has survived crises before. One of the most serious was in 1995, when AR2 concluded that “the balance of the evidence” suggested humans are responsible for global warming. This was challenged by representatives of some fossil-fuel-producing countries and oil and gas companies. But the organization’s scientists stood firm, often at great personal cost. Most IPCC-sponsoring governments backed the scientists, and the crisis eventually passed.

The current crisis is more serious because it concerns the IPCC’s very survival. Ideally, governments would come together again and ensure that the organization is properly funded. One way to resolve the matter would be to replace the current process of ad hoc voluntary contributions with multi-year budgetary commitments, similarly to those used to fund many other UN agencies. Support from non-governmental sources should also be considered.

The timing of the next assessment report must be resolved. But the dispute must not be allowed to distract from the most important matter of all: ensuring the continued survival of the IPCC itself.

#586. The homeless man living in front of a London mega-mansion

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Anders Fernstedt lives in London without any money. The Swedish native has built a most unusual home under the porch of a house worth over €200 million. How did that happen?

There's a lot of stopping and staring in Knightsbridge. This part of central London is within a stone's throw of Buckingham Palace, Hyde Park and Harrods, bringing inquisitive tourists in droves.

While it may not divert quite as many eyeballs as the seat of the British monarchy, a curious collection of plants, garden umbrellas, shopping bags and children's toys filling a building's entrance causes many a curious glance.

The peculiar arrangement on a grand portico is what Anders Fernstedt, a man from Sweden who fell on hard times, has been calling home for more than three years already.

That building hosting his makeshift setup was, just a few years ago, London's most expensive house.

The mega-mansion at 2-8A Rutland Gate sold in 2020 for a then-record £210 million (€244 million, $278 million) to Hui Ka Yan, the founder of China's Evergrande group, who was sentenced to life in prison last month.

Hui never moved in and the house was registered under his wife's name. The freezing of her assets means it can't be seized by liquidators and the house is in a state of limbo.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

So too was Fernstedt when he first stumbled across it. "I just thought, it would be a shelter for the night. I'm an avid camper, like an amateur botanist. I'm not afraid of nature," he told DW.

Fernstedt has never been inside the property, which appears to be in a state of disrepair. Instead, he gradually built his home in the portico, where grand columns guard the 45 rooms, indoor swimming pool and 116 windows. Year round he sleeps under the portico roof and a large umbrella which provides a hidden nook in which he's placed mattresses and bedding.

"I haven't had a bad night's sleep for as long as I can remember. And that goes for four seasons. It's not cold in the winter, and because I don't have walls, I get the breeze in the heat," he said.

"My conceit when I started was that sort of fake dream. Oh, I'm just a boy, my parents are in the house, everything's normal, I just asked them for permission to camp on the balcony."

Fernstedt was raised by his mother in Sweden before embarking on a range of careers at home and in the US, building a name for himself in the tech world.

In 2016, he moved to England where he worked as a journalist and fact checker at publications including The Economist, before work dried up around the time of the COVID pandemic.

A share in a tech company from his days in the US gave Anders a nest egg he relied on. But it couldn't last forever and he found himself living in a tent and then temporary accommodation, where he experienced violence and brushed up against people with severe addictions.

"Perhaps in this contemporary world, the biggest curiosity about my lifestyle is I'm completely off money," he said.

Fernstedt has built relationships with bakeries, cafes and florists in which he gets unused food, flowers for his home and use of power. He also makes use of a homeless charity in nearby Victoria for showers, clothing donations and socializing. But he's also made himself a broadly accepted part of one of London's most affluent neighborhoods.

"This is a very sophisticated neighborhood. I'd stayed for a few weeks and I knew everybody knew that I was here. And I thought, how can I sort of convey my presence without being present? And I thought, my constituency has to be the neighbors' children and grandchildren. Because if they plead my case at the kitchen table, my prospects improve," he said, by way of explaining the toys that line his abode.

"It is, in a way, a squirrel's nut collection," he added, when asked if he's worried about leaving his possessions out in the open. "I have so many nuts that I won't notice when something disappears."

There are some neighbors who do object to his presence, but Anders does his best to keep his home neat and his life quiet. Indeed, many others feel his presence prevents the house being a target for thieves or vandals. Overall though, he's found the community welcoming.

"Sometimes they introduce themselves asking what might I want or need. And my stock answer being: 'well, what you just gave me, a little bit of normal time, right? And neighborly banter'," he said. "Sometimes I'll be given food and very elegant Italian dinner jackets and clothes have arrived on a few occasions."

Not all homeless people in London have found such a stable lifestyle. Homeless charity Crisis estimates that there are over 200,000 people classified as homeless in England's capital, where "4,392 people were recorded sleeping rough in London between April and June, up from 4% on the same time last year. This is up 58% compared to 10 years ago."

According to government figures, there were 105,138 empty homes in London in 2025, or 1 in every 37 homes. Andy Burnham, who became British Prime Minister in July, has since vowed to offer "every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With such an enormous price tag, even after six years of being abandoned, Fernstedt knows that the house he lives at could potentially become untenable at virtually any moment.

But over the last few years, it's given him something he craved when pitching up his tent or being moved from one scary temporary residence to the next.

"I'm no longer really worried that I'll cycle around the corner and everything will be gone. Because I've been here so long, I'm free of worrying now, and if we worry too much, we won't be happy."

#565. Could measuring immune health reshape medical care?

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hugo J. W. L. Aerts is director of the Artificial Intelligence in Medicine Program, Mass General Brigham, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA, and a professor at Maastricht University, Maastricht, the Netherlands.

Nicolai J. Birkbak is a professor of cancer evolution and bioinformatics in the Department of Clinical Medicine, Aarhus University, Aarhus, Denmark, and in the Department of Molecular Medicine, Aarhus University Hospital.

John S. Tsang is the founding director of the Yale Center for Systems and Engineering Immunology, Yale School of Medicine, New Haven, Connecticut, USA, and a professor in the departments of Immunobiology and Biomedical Engineering, Yale University.

Eric J. Topol is a professor and executive vice-president of Scripps Research, La Jolla, California, USA.

The immune system is central to human health. When it fails, people can become more susceptible to infection and cancer. When misdirected, it can attack the body’s own tissues. And as it ages, it can contribute to chronic disease.

People of the same age can have strikingly distinct immune systems, shaped by genetics and by environmental and lifestyle factors, including air pollution, smoking, diet and past infections1,2. Growing evidence suggests that variation in the immune system’s ‘biological age’ — the rate at which it has aged, which is distinct from chronological age — matters for health. This variation has been linked to neurodegeneration, cancer and mortality risk3.

Immune cells have a surprising role in exercise endurance

Immune cells have a surprising role in exercise endurance

Yet, clinicians have no routine way of measuring how healthy someone’s immune system is. That’s because the immune system is a dynamic network that can change over time. It involves specialized organs that support immune-cell development and function, as well as immune cells that can circulate throughout the body and reside in tissues4. Signalling molecules, such as cytokines and chemokines, allow these immune cells and tissues to communicate.

Clinical tests provide only a fragmented picture of the immune system. A physician might examine an individual’s white blood cell count to establish whether circulating immune cells are at unusually high or low levels. They might also measure blood biomarkers such as C-reactive protein, which can indicate inflammation. But neither measurement is specific to a particular health condition, and they do not indicate whether the immune system as a whole is resilient or in decline, or if it is capable of mounting an effective response to infections and other challenges.

But advances in immunology, molecular profiling, medical imaging and artificial intelligence are opening up fresh possibilities for measuring the state of people’s immune systems. The stage is set for researchers to develop the immunome: a comprehensive characterization of immune health across cells, tissues, organs and molecular interactions (see ‘Defining the immunome’).

A raft of assays can provide information about the state of a person’s immune system.

Large-scale analysis of circulating proteins and antibodies

Patterns of immune signalling and antibody recognition beyond individual clinical markers

Types, abundance and molecular states of immune cells

Diversity and composition of immune-cell populations

Detection of quantifiable features from medical images of immune-related organs

Structural and compositional features of the thymus, spleen and bone marrow

Locations of immune cells and how they are organized relative to other cells

Measurements of immune-system activity before and after immune challenges

Strength, timing and persistence of responses to challenges such as vaccination

Long-term modelling of immune health using artificial intelligence

Several types of data can be combined to predict how ageing and disease change a person’s immune health

Research initiatives such as the Human Immunome Project, which one of us (J.S.T.) co-leads, are beginning to provide the data needed. What remains unclear is whether this information could be used to improve patient care, and how that could be achieved. Which measurements best capture clinically important aspects of a person’s immune health? How stable are these variables over time? And, most importantly, can assessing them improve clinical decision-making and, ultimately, disease outcomes?

Measuring every aspect of the immune system will not be feasible for every person. Instead, researchers should try to identify key features that can be readily assessed in the clinic to flag aspects of the immune system that are weakened, or declining quickly when they shouldn’t be. Such assessments could open avenues for disease prevention, treatment guidance and methods to monitor interventions.

For instance, these features might enable physicians to recognize cases of accelerated immune ageing and spot individuals who need close disease monitoring. For cancer treatment, measures of immune health could help to identify people who are most likely to benefit from therapies that rely on the immune system5,6, as well as those with a high risk of adverse reactions.

Such measurements could also help researchers to understand why people of similar ages and apparently similar health sometimes have substantially different responses to the same infection — a phenomenon that was apparent during the COVID-19 pandemic. Antibody responses to the same vaccine likewise vary widely between individuals2,7. If this variability could be measured, clinicians could use it to tailor preventive measures, treatments and monitoring to an individual’s immune system.

Researchers, health-care systems and funders must work to find the smallest, most scalable set of measurements that can capture meaningful differences in immune function and guide clinical decisions. Here, we outline a road map for moving the immunome from the laboratory to the clinic.

First, scientists should generate longitudinal data sets using large research populations and biobanks. Gaining a full understanding of immune health will require measuring several components of the immune system alongside broader indicators of health and disease in the same people over time.

Analysis of genes and gene expression in single cells from large research populations and biobanks could help researchers to understand which immune-cell groups are present in distinct populations. This could reveal which genes and signalling pathways are active in particular populations of cells, and what combination of markers best distinguishes between healthy, declining and dysfunctional immune states2,3,8. Analysing blood proteins can indicate whether a person is experiencing inflammation and whether their immune system has been activated. And studying the receptors on immune cells called lymphocytes can reveal the diversity of cells available to recognize threats. These receptors determine which pathogenic antigens the cells will identify; greater diversity generally allows the immune system to detect a broader range of threats.

The Moderna cancer vaccine offers hope — now we must speed up personalized therapies

The Moderna cancer vaccine offers hope — now we must speed up personalized therapies

Researchers must also study how the immune system changes over time to respond to challenges. Studying people before and after they are vaccinated is one standardized way to do this. It’s already clear that a person’s immune state before vaccination can predict the strength and characteristics of the immune response that follows2,9. The task now is to find out whether a person’s response to routine vaccination could provide a practical read-out of their immune competence10, and whether it would be possible to modify the immune health of an individual before interventions such as vaccination or cancer immunotherapy to improve their response2,5.

Data sets used to probe the immunome must represent the diversity of human immunity, because genetics and environmental factors alter immune states1. For example, malaria vaccine efficacy can differ markedly between populations across continents7,11. Yet, many existing immune-profiling data sets are concentrated in populations from high-income nations. When studying diverse populations, researchers around the world should use the same protocols so that results from various regions can be compared.

A big challenge will be making sense of complex data sets. AI tools can identify patterns across thousands of immune measurements, but those patterns might reflect differences between populations, laboratories or technologies rather than underlying immune health. Models will therefore need to be tested across independent populations and over time to establish which signals are robust and clinically meaningful.

Scientists working on the Human Immunome Project are developing and applying AI approaches to immunome data collected from various populations. An important goal for the project is to create reference maps and foundation models that scientists can use for tasks such as identifying small, manageable sets of measurements that would be useful in clinical settings.

With large-scale data in hand, researchers should work towards simplification. The success of the field should be judged not by how many immune variables can be measured, but by whether it is possible to improve clinical decision-making with just a small, manageable set of them. Tests used in the clinic would ideally be cheap and should not put extra demands on patients. Before any AI tools can be used routinely, they will need to be tested across a range of hospitals and populations. Researchers must establish whether a tool’s outputs truly improve treatment decisions.

One example of a tool that might be useful in the clinic is an AI model capable of extracting information about immune health from routine blood tests and clinical information such as age, sex, body weight and medical history. In a study published last year6, such an approach was able to predict health outcomes after immunotherapy treatment for people with cancer.

#550. Bulgaria seeks suspects in Germany after Starlink sabotage

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

A Bulgarian court has issued arrest warrants for two young German nationals suspected of setting fire to Starlink antennas. The case is reminiscent of another in Poland, which Warsaw says was orchestrated by Russia.

Bulgaria on Monday issued European arrest warrants against two 19-year-old German nationals, saying it suspected their involvement in the sabotage of a series of Starlink antennas near the capital Sofia.

"The evidence gathered makes it possible to conclude that there are reasonable grounds to suspect the involvement of the two defendants," the court in Sofia rules, granting a request from prosecutors.

Ukraine's military uses Starlink's military-grade satellite internet service Starshield for battlefield communications amid Russia's invasion.

Bulgaria does not directly border Ukraine, but it is on the Black Sea, one of the flashpoints of the conflict. A similar case in Poland, which does directly border Ukraine, led to a total of four arrests last week, also in Germany.

The two teenage suspects are accused of deliberately setting fire to the antennas on the evening of October 9.

Of 18 in a mountainous region south of Sofia, three were destroyed entirely, two were partially burned and three more were damaged, according to prosecutors.

Prosecutors say the suspects entered from Serbia in a car with German license plates, claiming to be tourists, staying just a few hours around the time of the alleged crime.

Plamen Tonchev, the head of Bulgaria's domestic intelligence agency DANS, said he was working on the assumption that it was deliberate sabotage and said other such acts could not be ruled out in future.

News of the arrests follow just a week after a total of four people were arrested in Germany, accused of sabotaging a Starlink satellite communications station in central Poland in late September.

German police detained three resident men and a woman, two of them Turkish nationals, early last week.

Polish officials said they believed that Russia was behind the sabotage attempt, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk calling it an act of "hybrid warfare."

The domestic intelligence agency also claimed that Russia had cooperated with organized crime elements in Germany on the alleged operation.

Meanwhile, in the Baltic, Lithuania's prime minister on Sunday said that Russia was likely behind an attempted arson attack on a company hosting communication hardware for Starlink satellites.
