#55. Turnout at Israel's election has reached a record high at the halfway stage

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Almost 45% of the electorate had voted by 2 p.m., the highest share since such records began in 1973. The highly anticipated vote is expected to be a close-fought contest, and perhaps even a stalemate.

Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election on October 27, 2026, and its aftermath:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

It's now 10 p.m. across Israel, which means that polling stations around the country either should have closed or should be making preparations to do so as the last people in line cast their ballots.

Exit polls should follow shortly on Israeli television. These have a fairly good reputation overall but of course are only projections.

Results will start to trickle in through the night and are unlikely to be finalized until Wednesday.

And of course, there's every chance that even once the dust has settled and the final results are in, we will have a longer wait until there's clarity about who might be able to form a coalition government.

In any case, stick with us and we'll keep you posted.

The Central Elections Committee has rejected a request by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and some other groups to extend voting beyond 10 p.m. (2000 UTC/GMT).

"High nationwide turnout across all sectors of society reflects strong public engagement in the democratic process, and no need to extend voting hours was identified," a commission statement said.

The committee noted, however, that this decision was based on the circumstances "as things stand," leaving open the possibility for matters to change.

For instance, voting hours have been extended in some areas, including a polling location used by Israeli settlers in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank, where a power outage led to an extension of the closing time from 8 p.m. to 10 p.m. Polling stations with fewer than 350 eligible voters typically close two hours earlier than larger polling stations in urban areas.

The commission has also said several times that anybody who started queueing before closing time will be given a chance to vote.

Artificial intelligence is emerging as a major factor in Israel's election campaign, with political parties using AI-generated videos, automated calls and online content on a large scale.

DW's Josh Axelrod examined the growing role of AI in the campaign, as researchers and analysts raise concerns about misleading content, bots and deepfakes ahead of the vote.

The expected high turnout means the number of votes needed to cross the 3.25% threshold to enter the Knesset, the Israeli parliament, is going to be higher, meaning smaller parties are at risk of not making it.

According to opinion polls from last week, the two parties that are on the threshold limit are Amcha Israel, a far-right party led by former military commander Ofer Winter, and the Reservists Party, which has not declared support for either main bloc.

Winter repeatedly said he intends to join a Netanyahu coalition, and a scenario in which his party doesn't make it to parliament puts Likud's chances of a future coalition at risk.

Either way, Israel's Central Elections Committee will have to make a decision on the matter within the hour.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Voter turnout reached 66.7%, or roughly two in every three eligible voters, by 6 p.m. local time, according to an update from the Central Elections Committee.

This remains the highest partial turnout figure since such records were first taken in 1973.

The level is only slightly clear of the previous high of 65.2% in 1973 and 1988 — but it quite considerably surpasses the 57.7% who had voted by this time in 2022.

And that figure had already been the highest 6 p.m. turnout of the 21st century before being surpassed today.

Arab voters could play a decisive role in Israel's election. With neither Benjamin Netanyahu nor Gadi Eisenkot expected to win a Knesset majority, Arab parties could become key to forming the next government.

Activists worked to boost voter turnout, especially among young voters.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu continued issuing appeals to supporters to go out and vote online as the day progressed.

One common theme was apparent in almost all of the posts: warnings about high turnout in Arab and to a lesser extent left-leaning communities.

"We're at war for our home," one of Netanyahu's posts read, using a phrase that appeared repeatedly in his messaging. "Muslim Brotherhood supporters are raiding the polling stations and stealing the elections. Go out and vote, recover it!!"

In another post he showed an image claiming to show a long line of voters queueing in Rahat, with a crowd of women wearing niqab coverings prominently visible at the front of the queue, suggesting that they were Muslim Palestinian voters.

Sami Abou Shahadeh, the leader of the Balad party, which is part of the alliance known as the Joint List, in turn called on his supporters to vote before the deadline expired, also highlighting similar appeals to voters from the leader of the far-right Jewish Power party, Itamar Ben-Gvir.

"There is one response to the incitement by Ben-Gvir and Netanyahu against the Arab citizens that has been going on all day: go out and vote for the Joint List!" he wrote.

The president of the German-Israeli Society, Green party politician Volker Beck, said in a TV interview on election day that he believed a change in leadership might be in Israel's interests.

"It would be good for Israel, if it were to come to a change, because I believe that [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu has squandered a great deal of trust in recent years, both in foreign and domestic policy," Beck said in an interview broadcast on sister channels RTL and ntv.

Beck, a Bundestag lawmaker for more than two decades with the Greens who was perhaps best known as a politician as a campaigner for LGBT rights and advocate of an uncompromising Israeli foreign policy, is not typically associated with stern criticism of Netanyahu or his government.

"Although he has also done some things right and has done some necessary things, a change is really needed" to allow Israel to recoup support among the international community, Beck said, as Netanyahu becomes an increasingly polarizing figure on the world stage.

He also criticized domestic efforts by the Likud-led government to reform the legal system and its influence over politics, saying this would "fundamentally change Israel's character, and should be stopped."

Beck said he hoped that a functioning majority would emerge from the vote, but acknowledged that pollsters anticipated a stalemate. In that scenario, he said, he would personally favor a national unity government incorporating all the major players.

But at present he thought the "divide between the two camps is so deep, that it really would be a bit of a masterstroke to be able to bring them together." He made a similar comment online, saying such a unity govermment "would be good" but was "not very likely."

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party wrote on the Telegram social media channel that it has submitted a request for polling stations to stay open later.

"Likud: We have submitted a request to extend the voting hours!" the post said.

It offered no further details, for instance, how long an extension it was seeking or whether it was to be nationwide or at individual polling stations.

The Ultra-Orthodox Shas party also joined the petition, according to the Times of Israel, saying: "The parties are trying to prevent a situation in which citizens waiting in line won’t be able to vote."

The main opposition Yashar party rejected the extension, saying: "No exceptional incident has occurred that would justify granting this request, which is intended to lay the groundwork for allegations challenging the integrity of the election, continuing the lies Netanyahu has been spreading since this morning."

Politicians of all stripes have been trying hard to mobilize voters for what's expected to be a tight race. Turnout has also been high so far, with long lines at some polling stations as a result of this.

Voting was already set to continue quite late into the night, with polling stations scheduled to close at 10 p.m. local time. Voters who are in line at polling stations at closing time will still be allowed to vote.

Polls show Israel's many young voters are more likely to vote for far-right parties, particularly Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party.

An opinion poll by Agam Labs at Jerusalem's Hebrew University predicts that supporters of Otzma Yehudit are younger than the average Israeli voter, with as many as a third voting for the first time.

Over 500,000 Israelis have reached voting age since the 2022 election. Of those voters, three in every four define themselves as right or center-right, according to a recent poll for Channel 12. The poll did not survey Palestinian citizens of Israel.

First-time voters were teenagers when Ben-Gvir joined Netanyahu's incumbent government in 2022, making up Israel's most far-right government to date.

A year later, they witnessed the Hamas-led October 7 terror attack which killed 1,200 Israelis, mostly civilians, and saw some 251 others taken hostage and brought to Gaza. The attack triggered a 2-year war on the Palestinian enclave that resulted in tens of thousands of Palestinians killed and intensified settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank. Hamas is designated as a terrorist group by several countries.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Previously, Otzma Yehudit's support was concentrated primarily among settlers in the occupied West Bank.

While security remained the dominant issue for Israeli voters, one topic was largely absent from the election campaign: a peace process with the Palestinians.

After years of conflict and failed negotiations, that debate has been pushed to the political margins.

Has Israeli society abandoned the idea of coexistence?

Avraham Burg, an Israeli writer and former Speaker of the Israeli Parliament, shares his insights with DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Turnout in Israel's election keeps rising. It reached a record 44.9% by 2 p.m. (1200 UTC), the Central Elections Commission said.

Some 3.29 million Israelis had cast their ballots by that point, commission head Dean Livne said.

It was the highest turnout recorded at that hour since the commission began collecting comparable statistics in 1973.

Gadi Eisenkot, the main challenger to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, urged voters on Tuesday to oust what he called the "worst government" in Israel's history and promised a more responsible style of leadership.

"There is a wind of change blowing in Israel, and this change will come into effect tonight at 10 p.m.," at which point polls close, he said after casting his own vote at a polling station in Holon, just south of Tel-Aviv.

"We will not lead Israel through division and scaremongering, but through unity and true love," he said. "We will win!"

Ahead of election day, Israeli pollsters had predicted a close race between Netanyahu's right-wing conservatives and Eisenkot's opposition bloc, with neither expected to win an outright majority.

"I call on all citizens of Israel to vote, not to buckle under the heat or the disruptions, to stick to the mission," said Eisenkot. "To replace tonight the worst government since the state was established."

Three years after the Hamas-led October 7 attacks exposed major flaws in Israeli security, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu  remains the dominant figure in Israel's political landscape. DW examines how many Israeli voters judge him more on his response to the crisis than on the failures that preceded it.

Experts point to security concerns, fear, Israel's conflicts on multiple fronts, and the absence of a clear challenger as key factors behind Netanyahu's resilience. The report also explores why international criticism can strengthen his support ahead of Israel's upcoming Knesset election.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Israel's Central Elections Committee said on Tuesday that "there are currently no indications of systematic tampering with ballot slips" after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused Arab-Israeli parties of "trying to steal the election."

Netanyahu made the allegation after casting his own ballot in Jerusalem while urging voters to choose his Likud party.

"We know what is at stake ... We cannot leave this battle here in the hands of the left and the Arab parties that want to bring an end to the Jewish state," he said.

Netanyahu has used Arab-Israeli parties throughout the election to stoke fears of a Palestinian state and mobilize voters for Likud.

"So no barbecues, don't go to the beach — go to the polling station and vote Likud."

Netanyahu had said that three senior officials from the opposition Ra'am party, which has an Arab Muslim voter base, had been arrested in southern Israel with envelopes full of cash.

The acting director general of the Central Elections Committee, Dean Livne, referred to the "unusual" incident with the envelopes in a press conference Tuesday morning but said that "police, even before people arrived at the polling stations, caught individuals who tried to bribe voters."

He said the unidentified suspects were not actually at polling stations and were caught near their homes, adding the matter was under investigation.

"There are no similar incidents of this kind across the country," he concluded. "This was a localized case."

Opposition parties, including that of Netanyahu's main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, have also complained that ballot papers were being defaced and stolen at polling stations.

#34. Mbappe apologizes as Chinese sponsors drop him and TV broadcasts are halted over Mao dictator remark

📅 Oct 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

French soccer star Kylian Mbappe has apologized after apparently referring to Mao Zedong as a dictator. Chinese sponsors have dropped him, while state television has suspended Spanish league broadcasts.

France striker Kylian Mbappe apologized after apparently referring to China's founding leader Mao Zedong as a dictator in a video that circulated online.

The controversy prompted three major Chinese companies to sever sponsorship ties with the Real Madrid forward, while Chinese state television suspended broadcasts of Spain's La Liga.

The controversy began when a video circulated showing Mbappe discussing his favorite internet meme featuring himself.

In the clip, apparently filmed ahead of an appearance on the French online talk show The Bridge, Mbappe referred to an image depicting his face superimposed on the body of "some guy ... I think he's a Chinese dictator."

The image appeared to depict Mao Zedong, who founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and ruled until his death in 1976. Jokes about country's former leader and descriptions of him as a dictator remain taboo.

Mbappe has previously been depicted as authoritarian leaders in online memes mocking his perceived influence over teammates and suggestions that he has the power to influence club decisions.

Mbappe has been nicknamed "the dictator" in the European press.

"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappe said in a statement.

"I apologize to everyone my words have upset. This was absolutely not my intention. I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry."

Chinese beverage company Dongpeng, dairy producer Mengniu and cheesemaker Milkground announced they were ending their partnerships with the French international.

In similarly worded statements, each said that they oppose "any words and actions that hurt national sentiment."

China Media Group, which oversees state broadcaster CCTV, also suspended broadcasts of La Liga matches and removed advertisements featuring Mbappe.

La Liga apologized for the controversy, saying Mbappe's comments were made in a personal capacity and did not represent the Spanish league.

Chinese state broadcaster CCTV subsequently said it would consider Mbappe's apology but would also judge his future actions.

In response to a question about the controversy, China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said that "words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."

Mao remains a revered figure in China, where public criticism of the former Communist leader is politically sensitive.

His rule was also marked by disastrous political campaigns, including the Great Leap Forward, which contributed to a famine that killed tens of millions of people.

The ruling Communist Party acknowledges some of his mistakes but maintains that his achievements outweighed them, making criticism of his legacy politically sensitive.

#5351. Mazda and Seiko Made a $439 Chronograph, but It's Only Sold in Japan

📅 Oct 27, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Mazda and Seiko are two very important Japanese companies; both exhibit true heritage and precision when it comes to car making and watchmaking. Between the two of them is an expansive back catalog that features some of the most iconic Japanese creations of all time.

So it wouldn’t come as a shock to anyone that these 2 companies would work together to create more icons, but this time in the form of a timekeeper. The latest collaboration model has just been launched in Japan, leaving the rest of the world in envy.

Mazda just dropped its newest collaboration timepiece with Seiko (BF9504), a chronograph that embodies what Mazda calls the “aesthetics of subtraction and condensed elegance.” Mazda says the BF9504 draws on its award-winning design language while keeping the functionality of a chronograph. Both brands wanted a minimalist design, free of unnecessary colors and decorations on the dial, while the red stopwatch second hand and crown serve as an accent.

One thing that makes this collaboration stand out from the others is that it’s the first to use curved Hardlex glass. The curved glass gives the design a 3D impression, and the glass itself has been further strengthened to resist scratches. The 3D glass also offers a unique viewing experience depending on the angle, which the designers were also aiming for.

The dial itself was inspired by Mazda’s clusters and meters, boasting excellent legibility. Its design contrasts black metal with red accents, and the font is called Mazda Type, an original to the brand. Another key detail is embedded on the watch: “ESTD 1920 HIROSHIMA, JAPAN.” This small detail shows just how long the Mazda story has been and how far it’s come.

The complete package includes two interchangeable straps in leather or steel. Even the watchbox is special, featuring a tri-color design that echoes the watch it houses. For the very lucky who can purchase the watch in Japan, it’ll cost 69,300 Japanese yen ($439 converted), and it will be available for order through dealers starting October 29.

As a fun fact, this model is the third collaboration between Mazda and Seiko; the first was in 2001, a vintage rotary-themed model. The most recent was a watch commemorating Mazda’s race team, the Mazda Spirit Racing model, which was sold last year.

#4857. Robinhood Chain brings in $26 million as crypto revenue rises 20% in Q3

📅 Oct 27, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

Crypto trading revenue excluding Robinhood Chain fell 6% from Q2, while prediction markets revenue climbed to $173 million.

Robinhood's crypto revenue jumped 20% from the previous quarter to $120 million, offsetting a decline in crypto trading revenue, the company reported Tuesday.

In its third-quarter earnings, Robinhood Chain brought in $26 million in its first quarter on mainnet after launching on July 1.

Excluding this, crypto transaction revenue fell 6% from the second quarter to $94 million, while total crypto revenue remained down 55% from a year earlier when crypto markets were nearing bull market highs.

Crypto trading volumes also ramped up from last quarter, rising 23% to $49.8 billion — $20.6 billion coming from the Robinhood app itself and $29.2 billion on Bitstamp, the exchange it acquired last year.

The company said Robinhood Chain, its layer 2 blockchain built on Arbitrum, processed more than $80 billion in DEX volume and made over $50 million in fees during the quarter.

Prediction markets also continued to add more revenue than crypto. Event contracts generated $173 million, up 11% from the previous quarter and more than 6x from a year earlier. That includes $28 million from Rothera, its joint exchange with Susquehanna.

Robinhood's total net revenue rose 12% year over year to a record $1.42 billion while net income fell 14% to $476 million.

Robinhood shares Robinhood Markets, Inc. (HOOD) fell 5.5% in after-hours trading to $89.22, leaving the stock down roughly 22% year-to-date.

#5142. Dell sees AI agent guardrails as a path to greater autonomy

📅 Oct 27, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

As enterprises put AI agents to work, they face a challenge: How can they give those systems more autonomy while keeping AI agent guardrails in place?

Security and resilience are becoming central considerations as enterprises decide which tasks to delegate to AI agents. Those decisions extend beyond individual actions to the data protection and cyber resilience capabilities that support the business, according to John Scimone (pictured), president and chief security officer of Dell Technologies Inc.

“The good news is, this is the best time to get it right,” Scimone said. “Organizations are today designing agents that are going to be working for years ahead. At that point of design is always the best time to get security done well, to get resilience done well. Security resilience by design for agentic is a huge opportunity.”

Scimone spoke with theCUBE’s Dave Vellante for the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how cyber resilience has replaced traditional disaster recovery, how security leaders brief boards and how much autonomy enterprises should give AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)

Business resilience once meant disaster recovery built around wildfires, hurricanes and grid outages. Today, a widespread cyberattack across an entire digital ecosystem is the more likely scenario, according to Scimone. Agents add a new dependency because work handed to software stops when the software does.

“What happens if these agents aren’t available?” Scimone said. “What happens if the data that the agents are deciding on is not available? A core part of your resilience posture has to contend with the notion that if our agents go down, our work is not happening.”

Companies are still cautious about letting agents act alone. A survey of 25 enterprise technology and security leaders  led by theCUBE Research’s Krista Case found that 19 had autonomous agents in production. None allowed those agents to perform high-risk actions without human approval.

“It doesn’t mean doing it willy-nilly and just throwing caution to the wind,” he said. “It means being very thoughtful around where can’t you fail, putting deterministic guardrails in place … and letting the business run. Right now, I’m seeing too much caution in the space on that front.”

Dell applies that discipline internally, giving every agent tight identity and access control, extensive logging and traceability of decisions and actions, Scimone explained. That groundwork matters because only four of the survey’s 25 respondents had tested an AI agent incident scenario. Dell has also expanded its cyber resilience tools and joined OpenAI Group PBC’s call for collective action on cyber defense.

Attackers have used AI for years but haven’t yet deployed it at full scale, according to Scimone. He expects that to change soon.

“We haven’t hit that curve that I do believe is coming, and in the coming quarters, not in the coming years,” he said.

Vellante pointed to one encouraging finding from the survey: Organizations granting agents bounded autonomy showed stronger recovery readiness than those relying solely on human approval. In Scimone’s view, AI agent guardrails designed up front let companies take more risk, not less.

“Organizations that design those governance systems upfront are going to be the ones, ironically, that can move the quickest and can take the most risk because they can do it confidently with the right insights and the right data to know that they’re not overstepping,” Scimone said. “At the same time, they’re not under-leaning.”

U.S. President Donald Trump is facing yet another court challenge to his tariff-driven war on trade, after an unbroken string of prior defeats that leave the future of his mercurial trade policy increasingly uncertain.

Last week, the same company that successfully challenged Trump’s global tariffs under the 1977 International Emergency Economic Powers Act filed suit against his latest attempt to reach back in time. At issue is Trump’s use of an obscure and never-used statute, Section 338 of the 1930 Trade Act, to punish Canada for its allegedly discriminatory behavior toward U.S. commerce.

U.S. President Donald Trump is facing yet another court challenge to his tariff-driven war on trade, after an unbroken string of prior defeats that leave the future of his mercurial trade policy increasingly uncertain.

Last week, the same company that successfully challenged Trump’s global tariffs under the 1977 International Emergency Economic Powers Act filed suit against his latest attempt to reach back in time. At issue is Trump’s use of an obscure and never-used statute, Section 338 of the 1930 Trade Act, to punish Canada for its allegedly discriminatory behavior toward U.S. commerce.

This new trade fight may not be as clear-cut as some of the prior Trump defeats in court, though.

The central thrust of the lawsuit challenging Sec. 338—part of the notorious Smoot-Hawley law that ushered in the Great Depression—is that the law was explicitly designed for a different world.

The statute, which had never been used and in fact was unknown even to many trade experts until Trump resurrected it, was designed to give the United States a way to push back against countries such as France and Great Britain that were discriminating against U.S. exports as part of “imperial preference”—a circling of the wagons that gave preferential treatment to colonies at the expense of global trade in the dawning days of the depression.

The statute was “all about imperial preferences,” said Sara Albrecht, the chairman and chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, which filed the lawsuit on behalf of a U.S. business harmed by Trump’s latest trade spat.

And even more clearly, the statute was meant to give the White House a tool to deter other countries from discriminating against U.S. exports—not a cudgel to wield against countries (such as Canada) whose tariffs on U.S. goods were dollar-for-dollar retaliation for Trump’s first round of trade restrictions.

“Retaliation is not discrimination,” Albrecht told Foreign Policy.

But even if the narrowly tailored 1930 statute were valid for modern-day trade fights, that doesn’t matter, the suit (and many scholars) argue, because Sec. 338 is—legally speaking—dead and buried.

That 1930 law has been updated and superseded not once but twice in later legislation, first through the 1962 Trade Act and later in Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act. Everything that was in the old statute was rehashed in more modern law—and, according to established legal doctrine, that Hoover-era law has arguably been implicitly repealed. What’s more, the updated version of the statute includes a lot more limits and safeguards, including formal investigation of alleged wrongdoing by other countries. The tool that Trump has turned to for his fourth bite at the apple would dodge all those limits.

“Congress did not intend to leave in place a parallel authority that would allow the President to impose the same remedies, for the same conduct, free of every one of those safeguards,” the plaintiffs argued in their lawsuit before the U.S. Court of International Trade.

The Trump administration has leaned heavily on that updated version of the statute—Sec. 301 of the 1974 Act—for many of its tariffs, from the first-term duties on Chinese exports to the second-term attempt to slap tariffs on every U.S. trading partner. (Those tariffs are also currently facing an uphill battle in court.)

But if Sec. 338 is still valid, scholars such as Philip Zelikow argue, then Sec. 301 cannot be. That would mean that the main weapon the Trump administration is relying on to continue global tariffs in the wake of this year’s Supreme Court setback is itself invalid: Trump cannot have his cake and eat it, too.

The whole battle over Trump’s tariffs comes at a time when the United States continues to pursue elusive trade deals with major partners, including Canada. Trump administration officials have said that a deal with Canada—with whom the United States has had a free-trade agreement since the 1990s—is close, but Canadian officials say a final agreement remains far off.

This latest clash over what seems to be an arcane relic of U.S. trade legislation is important because of the way that the Trump administration has sought to weaponize trade to a much greater degree in the second term than in the first. During Trump’s first term, his administration relied on relatively targeted and legally defensible authorities to slap tariffs on big trading partners.

But starting early in his second term, Trump sought to hike tariffs on every country in the world, starting with a novel use of a Carter administration-era law that had never been used to impose tariffs—and with good reason, as the Supreme Court later ruled. That 1977 law doesn’t give the president the power to levy tariffs, even for a self-proclaimed national-security “emergency,” such as a half-century of persistent trade deficits.

Undeterred, the Trump administration replaced the outlawed first batch of tariffs with a new tranche under a provision of the 1974 Trade Act. That, too, was struck down by courts, but it had expired by then anyway.

So the administration reached for a third option, also under the 1974 law, which hit 99 percent of U.S. trade with tariffs on the grounds that every U.S. trading partner was lax on combating forced labor in supply chains. That attempt, too, is under legal challenge, and it’s likely to be struck down.

And then Trump reached even further back in the history books to find a way to punish Canada for retaliating against his previous rounds of tariffs by invoking, for the first time, a statute that even protectionist President Herbert Hoover was loath to sign into law.

The irony is that all of Trump’s efforts to hike import duties paid by U.S. businesses and consumers by every means possible is that they have conspicuously failed to achieve any of their stated goals.

Exports are falling and imports are rising, widening the very trade deficit that Trump said was a national emergency. Tariffs have failed to drive a manufacturing renaissance, either in employment or the construction of new factories. Nor have the tariffs been a reliable source of additional revenue for a government saddled with a huge budget deficit and $40 trillion in debt: Net tariff revenues as a share of overall revenues are actually lower than at any time in the past decade, in part because courts have made the U.S. government refund tariffs collected illegally.

And increasing the price of nearly everything from nearly every country in the world has exacerbated inflation, which is a problem for the Trump administration as it tries to grapple with an affordability crisis ahead of the midterm elections. U.S. inflation is now running at 3.7 percent year-on-year, higher than when Trump took office, fueled by higher energy prices (fruit of the Iran war), tariffs, and the artificial intelligence build-out. That self-inflicted higher inflation makes a serious case for the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates this week—the very opposite course of what Trump has advocated for years.

The through line of all of Trump’s second-term tariff fights, from the Rose Garden “Liberation Day” tariff announcement that slapped duties on penguins to his efforts to resuscitate moribund trade relics to punish Canada, is that Congress is missing in action. Despite a handful of tepid attempts early in Trump’s second term to wrest back the constitutional powers of taxation from the White House, there have been no serious legislative efforts to reverse nearly a century of congressional delegation of trade authority to the executive branch.

“If Congress were doing its job, we wouldn’t be in this place,” said Albrecht of the Liberty Justice Center.

That may soon change. U.S. midterm elections are only a week away, and Democrats are widely predicted to win back the House of Representatives and perhaps even control of the Senate. Trump’s one-man war on trade (and trade law) may soon have an expiration date.

Keith Johnson is a staff writer at Foreign Policy covering geoeconomics and energy. Bluesky: @kfj-fp.bsky.social X: @KFJ_FP

#5623. Judge who apologized to accused would-be Trump assassin lights up DOJ in Hunter Biden FBI case

📅 Oct 27, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Fox News correspondent David Spunt reports on two former FBI officials being charged by the DOJ with lying in the investigation into Hunter Biden's taxes.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia M. Faruqui, who previously apologized to a man accused of attempting to assassinate President Donald Trump, rebuked the Justice Department on Tuesday over its attempt to bring new obstruction charges against two former FBI officials without first securing judicial approval.

Former FBI officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides were arrested last week after the Department of Justice accused the duo of misrepresenting their involvement in investigations concerning former President Joe Biden’s son, Hunter Biden, in statements to Congress.

Hours before prosecutors were scheduled to defend their original allegations at a preliminary hearing, where the government must establish probable cause, the DOJ filed a superseding criminal complaint seeking to add new charges against the former officials. The new complaint sought to add felony obstruction allegations against the former officials while softening some of the language prosecutors had used to describe their involvement in the Hunter Biden investigations.

Faruqui sharply criticized the DOJ for filing an unsigned and unsworn criminal complaint in the middle of the night without first obtaining judicial approval.

WHO IS JUDGE ZIA FARUQUI? WHAT WE KNOW ABOUT THE FEDERAL MAGISTRATE WHO APOLOGIZED TO COLE ALLEN

Magistrate Judge Zia M. Faruqui speaks before a debate between incarcerated students and James Madison University students on the topic of abolishing life without parole at Prettyman Federal Courthouse in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 22, 2024. (Craig Hudson for The Washington Post via Getty Images)

"I think they should have filed nothing," Faruqui said, according to reports from inside the courtroom. "They never had complaints filed on their record that are unsigned, waiting for a judge to make a probable cause finding. I think that it is inappropriate and harms the defendant. I'm frustrated that I got it in the middle of the night, but I'm much more concerned that it's filed on the public record."

"Why today on this one case have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases?" Faruqui asked the DOJ. "What is it? It appears that – it makes it look like the United States is afraid of me trying to find probable cause."

John Borchert, a prosecutor from the U.S. Attorney's Office in Washington, D.C., said it was the first time he had filed new charges against someone without going through judicial review.

Faruqui rejected the superseding complaint because prosecutors had not secured the required judicial authorization, allowing the preliminary hearing to proceed on the original allegations that Floris and Benavides lied to Congress. Floris’ lawyers argued that the changes in language between the two documents calls into question the factual basis of the DOJ’s case.

JUDGE WHO APOLOGIZED TO WHCA SHOOTING SUSPECT WAS APPOINTED BY COURT FULL OF ANTI-TRUMP JUDGES

Hunter Biden and former FBI official Nikki Floris. (AP Photo/Susan Walsh; AP Photo/Eric Thayer)

In the superseding complaint, prosecutors described Benavides and Floris as having been "involved in" the Foreign Influence Task Force's work concerning Hunter Biden, a softer characterization than the original complaint's suggestion that they had been at the "center" of those activities. Floris, who was previously said to have been involved in "scores of conversations" related to Biden’s son, is now only accused of participating in "conversations."

In what may have been a reference to the recently unsealed charges against former FBI Director James Comey, Faruqui said that moving on a superseding complaint without a probable cause finding "would be like charging someone by information... but in a complaint context."

"If you want a superseding complaint, like every other case that’s happened in this district, we will have a judge make a probable cause finding," the judge said. "Not send me something in the middle of the night and expect that it gets done."

Faruqui has previously faced criticism from conservatives over his support for diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives, criticism of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and positions on pretrial detention. He also drew backlash after apologizing to Cole Allen, the man accused of attempting to assassinate President Donald Trump at the 2026 White House Correspondents' Association Dinner, and criticizing the government's use of five-point restraints against him.

"To me, it’s extremely disturbing that he was put in five-point restraints, a person with no criminal history," the judge said about Allen at a hearing earlier this year. "It’s troubling. I never heard of one Jan. 6 defendant who was put in five-point restraints or in a safe cell. If the only way to keep him safe is the most punitive thing, that’s a problem."

The DOJ has also been questioned for charging via complaint rather than through a grand jury, a procedural shortcut usually reserved for imminent threats to public safety.

DEMOCRATS HAVE ‘DIRTY HANDS’ OVER COMPLAINTS ABOUT OMAR RAID WEEKS BEFORE ELECTION, EX-PROSECUTOR SAYS

Critics have questioned the timing of the charges, with midterm elections being just days away when news of the two former officials’ arrests broke.

Floris’ lawyers have similarly argued that the timing and content of the charges are meant to engineer publicity.

"What is going on at the D.C. U.S. Attorney's Office? In the middle of the night, the government filed an unsigned and unsworn complaint attempting to fix the issues with their original charge against Ms. Floris and adding a new charge just as meritless as the first one," said Floris' legal team in a statement provided to CBS News.

"In our combined decades of DOJ service, we have never seen or even heard of something like this being filed," they went on. "That's because the public lodging of criminal charges must be authorized by the grand jury, a judge, or the defendant herself. Here, the government has taken that power for itself in a desperate attempt to delay our client's right to challenge the charges in court and litigate this case in the media, rather than the courtroom. We have asked to address this outrageous government conduct against a decorated public servant at today's court hearing."

Legal teams for Floris and Benavides, as well as the DOJ, did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

#4782. Robinhood Misses Q3 Earnings as Crypto Revenue Rises and Prediction Market Bets Grow

📅 Oct 27, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Robinhood Misses Q3 Earnings as Crypto Revenue Rises and Prediction Market Bets Grow

Robinhood, the trading app where more than 28 million people keep money to buy stocks and crypto and now bet on sports and elections, reported third-quarter revenue of $1.42 billion billion on Tuesday, missing the roughly $1.43 billion Wall Street expected

Earnings came in at $0.51 per share, missing the $0.55 analysts projected and down from $0.61 a year ago. Earnings per share is profit divided by the number of shares outstanding, and it is the figure investors use to call a quarter a beat or a miss.

Robinhood is the app that brought commission-free trading to a generation of first-time investors, which makes its quarterly report one of the clearest readings of what ordinary people are doing with their money. When customers trade more, deposit more or pile into new products, the shift shows up in these numbers.

Net income was $476 million, down 14% from $556 million a year earlier and 17% from $573 million in the second quarter. The quarter included a $67 million unrealized loss, meaning a drop in value on paper, on Robinhood Ventures Fund I, which cost $0.07 per share. Adjusted earnings per share, which exclude certain items, came to $0.60, down 3% from a year ago.

Event contracts, the yes-or-no bets that pay out $1 if a game, an election or an economic report goes a certain way, brought in $173 million, up from $156 million in the second quarter, when they overtook crypto revenue for the first time. Customers traded a record 16.4 billion of them, more than seven times a year earlier.

“I believe we’re at the very beginning of a prediction market supercycle,” CEO Vlad Tenev said in December last year, when Robinhood added NFL player contracts and parlay-style combos that pay only if every outcome hits.

Crypto trading revenue rose to $120 million from $100 million in the second quarter, but remained down 55% from the $268 million Robinhood earned in the third quarter of 2025. Customers traded $50 billion in crypto during the quarter, down 38% from a year earlier, with $21 billion on the Robinhood app and $29 billion through Bitstamp, the crypto exchange it acquired

Robinhood Chain went live on July 1 as a layer-2 network, meaning a blockchain that runs on top of Ethereum to make transactions cheaper and faster. Its first weeks were driven by meme coins, joke-themed tokens, rather than the tokenized stocks it was built for, which are digital versions of company shares that trade on a blockchain.

By the end of August the chain had earned about $3.13 million in fees over 30 days, more than Ethereum and Base, which came in at $2.47 million and $2.89 million.

Hours before the report, Robinhood announced a deal with Ripple that brings RLUSD, a stablecoin (a crypto token designed to stay worth one dollar), to Robinhood Chain and Bitstamp, with an in-app rollout planned later this year. RLUSD has a market value above $2.5 billion, and Ripple will also supply Robinhood’s treasury software and lending for Bitstamp traders.

Robinhood shares closed Tuesday at about $94.61 and slipped in after-hours trading- The stock is down roughly 18% this year and about 37% below its 52-week high of $150.47.

Robinhood narrowed its 2026 outlook for adjusted operating expenses and stock-based pay to $2.675 billion to $2.75 billion, trimming the top of the $2.675 billion to $2.775 billion range it set in July.

#4671. Treasury's Bessent sees crypto as America's next tool for keeping the U.S. dollar on top

📅 Oct 27, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said digital assets could help strengthen the U.S. dollar's global dominance as technology becomes an increasingly important source of American economic influence.

Speaking Tuesday at Ripple's Swell conference with CEO Brad Garlinghouse, Bessent argued that the power behind the world's reserve currencies during history derived from military strength, but it’s increasingly shifting toward technological leadership.

"We will keep our military umbrella, but I think more and more it's becoming a technology umbrella," Bessent said.

He pointed to the growing divide between U.S. and Chinese technology ecosystems, where countries and companies face choices over whose artificial intelligence systems and semiconductor technology to adopt. Bessent said he sees digital assets as part of that competition, with the financial infrastructure countries may choose influencing the U.S. dollar’s reach.

"I think that digital assets are going to be no different, and we are going to win in the digital asset stack, and that's gonna continue to fortify the [U.S.] dollar," he said.

His remarks offered a broader rationale for the administration of President Donald Trump’s push to bring crypto businesses onshore, framing digital assets not just as a financial market but as part of the infrastructure that could sustain U.S. economic influence. The administration has already secured passage of the GENIUS Act, which established a federal regulatory framework for stablecoins, cryptocurrencies designed to maintain a fixed value against fiat currencies like the U.S. dollar.

Bessent argued that stablecoins could reinforce the dollar's position by expanding access to U.S. currency in countries where local currencies face inflation or sharp swings in value.

More than 90% of stablecoins are backed by U.S. dollars, he said, and their issuers often hold U.S. government securities as reserves. As adoption grows, demand for those assets could rise, creating another source of financing for the federal government.

"I think it's gonna be an important source of funding for the Treasury," Bessent said.

Bessent pushed back against the idea that stablecoins would merely replace dollars people already hold, arguing that they could reach new users in emerging markets who want to protect their savings from currency devaluation.

"I think we are opening up new markets all around the world," he said.

However, the White House’s broader push to regulate crypto markets suffered a setback after Congress failed to pass the Clarity Act, which would have established a federal framework for the industry.

Bessent called the failure a disappointment but said the Treasury Department could work with regulatory agencies like the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) to advance oversight through agency action.

"At Treasury, we have a lot of convening powers," he said, describing the SEC and CFTC as “great partners” in forming a regulatory framework that could serve as a model for other countries.

The agencies' regulatory efforts could provide more clarity for crypto firms, though rules adopted by regulators would lack the permanence of legislation.

Bessent also addressed the industry's concerns about debanking, a term used to describe financial institutions cutting off services to crypto businesses, sometimes allegedly under regulatory pressure.

He said the Clarity Act would have helped prevent a return to such practices but argued that regulatory safeguards could still offer protection.

"I think we can set up regulatory best practices, guardrails that will prevent that from happening again," Bessent said.

#4762. Quantum fears already limiting Bitcoin’s growth, Stacks founder says

📅 Oct 27, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Speaking on Cointelegraph’s Chain Reaction podcast, Muneeb Ali warned that uncertainty over Bitcoin’s quantum security could deter institutional investors.

Concerns about quantum computing are slowing institutional investment in Bitcoin, according to Stacks founder Muneeb Ali, who warned that the network needs a credible roadmap for security upgrades to restore investor confidence.

“There is already a ceiling on the growth of Bitcoin because of quantum fears,” Ali said during an interview on Cointelegraph’s Chain Reaction podcast. He argued that uncertainty could lead risk-averse institutional investors to delay large Bitcoin purchases until developers establish a credible path toward quantum-resistant security.

Stacks is a Bitcoin layer-2 network designed to bring smart contracts and decentralized applications to Bitcoin. Ali co-founded the project, which uses Bitcoin as its underlying settlement layer.

Chain Reaction Podcast. Source: Cointelegraph

Ali warned that Bitcoin could enter a riskier period if developers fail to make meaningful progress toward quantum-resistant security by 2028. He said upgrades typically take years to implement, with additional time needed for users to move their holdings to new addresses.

Ali pointed to 2030 as a target for transitioning to quantum-resistant security, citing guidance from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). He suggested advances in artificial intelligence could accelerate the development of quantum computers, potentially bringing that timeline forward to 2029.

Ali acknowledged that some Bitcoin proponents believe the quantum computing threat remains distant and concerns are overblown. He argued, however, that disagreements over the urgency of the threat could themselves undermine investor confidence, particularly without a credible upgrade roadmap.

Related: Justin Sun says Tron’s post-quantum cryptography has gone live on testnet

Despite his concerns, Ali said a sufficiently powerful quantum computer would more likely emerge from a major research laboratory than an unknown attacker. He suggested companies such as Google or Microsoft would have little incentive to use the technology to steal Bitcoin, given the potential legal consequences.

Ali also said a quantum security threat to Bitcoin would affect the broader cryptocurrency industry, even projects developing their own protections. “If Bitcoin gets hit, everyone gets hit downstream as well,” he said.

Meanwhile, developers are exploring ways to protect Bitcoin against quantum attacks. In September, StarkWare reported that researchers had reduced the estimated computing cost of preparing an experimental quantum-resistant Bitcoin transaction by 79%, following a weeklong optimization challenge.

The approach requires no changes to Bitcoin’s consensus rules, but the latest cost reductions have been demonstrated only in benchmark tests. StarkWare has described the technology as a last-resort measure and continues to advocate for a protocol-level upgrade as a longer-term solution.

#4682. Robinhood's crypto revenue fell 55% from last year, but topped Street forecasts

📅 Oct 27, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Robinhood's HOOD$94.61·Market Closed third-quarter cryptocurrency trading business was down 55% from last year but still topped Street forecasts.

Crypto transaction revenue dropped to $120 million in the third quarter, according to the company's earnings report released Tuesday. That was down from about $267 million in the same period last year, but ahead of Wall Street analysts’ expectations of $114.1 million.

That left crypto accounting for just 8.4% of Robinhood's $1.42 billion in total quarterly revenue, compared with roughly 21% a year earlier.

The decline came as customers traded less crypto across Robinhood's platforms. Total crypto trading volume fell 38% to $50 billion, including $21 billion through the Robinhood app, down 48%, and $29 billion through crypto exchange Bitstamp, down 28%.

The slump in crypto trading revenue stood in contrast to Robinhood's broader business. Total revenue rose 12% year-over-year to $1.424 billion, helped by growth in options, equities and prediction markets. Street estimates had been for $1.43 billion.

Options trading generated $399 million in revenue, up 31%, while equities revenue climbed 41% to $121 million. Prediction markets brought in $173 million, more than six times the year-earlier figure.

Third-quarter EPS of $0.51 was less than consensus forecasts for $0.55.

Despite weaker crypto trading, Robinhood continued to build out its digital asset business.

The company said Robinhood Chain, its blockchain network, processed more than $80 billion in decentralized exchange trading volume and generated over $50 million in chain fees during its first quarter operating on mainnet.

Those fees reflect activity on the blockchain and should not be confused with Robinhood's reported crypto transaction revenue. The company did not disclose how much of the chain fees it recognized as revenue.

Shares of the company were down about 5% in post-market trading.

📅 Oct 27, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Re:Build, the Massachusetts-based manufacturing accelerator that spun out EV startup Slate Auto in 2023, has raised $2.1 billion

The company said Tuesday that it will use the funding to “expand Re:Build’s capacity to manufacture hard tech products and launch new industrial startups,” which will “ensure the most innovative products can be made in America for generations to come.” The investment was led by General Catalyst and JPMorganChase’s Strategic Investment Group. Other investors weren’t disclosed.

The funding round comes as increasing attention and capital is flowing to the idea of building up manufacturing and supply chains in the United States, especially as a hedge away from China.

“We started Re:Build because the deindustrialization of America is an economic failure and national security risk,” Re:Build co-founder Jeff Wilke said in a statement. “This capital allows Re:Build to go faster and further than would otherwise be possible, and build a great manufacturing business and a platform for American industrial leadership. The products and companies emerging from our ecosystem prove we can help restore America’s industrial might.”

General Catalyst’s CEO Hemant Taneja echoed those sentiments in a statement saying, “General Catalyst has long believed that rebuilding American industrial capacity is one of the most important economic and national security imperatives of our time.”

Taneja added: “To compete with China, re-industrialize the U.S., and revitalize the towns and jobs that have been left behind, we need platform companies that can operate at genuine scale—and we need our innovation ecosystem to learn how to build hardware again.”

Founded in 2020, Re:Build bills itself as “America’s answer to Shenzhen,” and it has numerous ties to Amazon. It was co-founded by Wilke, who was Amazon’s former commercial CEO. Wei Gao, a longtime Amazon VP and technical adviser to Bezos, is Re:Build’s chief digital and product officer. Multiple other Re:Build executives also worked for the e-commerce giant.

Re:Build claims to have “launched hundreds of products and production systems” over its six-year existence. The company tends to operate two ways. It enters partnerships with industrial companies to “design, engineer, and manufacture products at scale across verticals including aerospace and defense.” It also incubates startups in “critical, underserved markets.”

Re:Build says its network of companies employs more than 2,100 people in the U.S. and houses more than 2.4 million square feet of manufacturing capacity.

Wilke and his co-founder Miles Arnone came up with the idea of Slate Auto in 2022, and decided to spin it out in order to help it attract more capital. The company has since gone on to raise at least $1.4 billion, including funding from Bezos’ family office, in an attempt to build an ultra low-cost, bare bones pickup truck that can be customized to a customer’s liking.

Disney's after-school lineup came with some after-school drama.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With plenty of new shows arriving on the 2026 TV premiere schedule, I've still got a soft spot for the Disney Channel shows that dominated my afternoons in the early 2000s. Even Stevens and Lizzie McGuire were two of the network's biggest hits, and I always assumed they coexisted pretty peacefully. Apparently, somebody forgot to tell Shia LaBeouf. According to his former co-star Christy Carlson Romano, he had a one-sided rivalry with Hilary Duff, and I genuinely had no idea.

Romano, who played LaBeouf's older sister Ren on Even Stevens, recently appeared on The Joe Vulpis Podcast, where the conversation turned to whether Disney Channel stars had beef with their Nickelodeon counterparts. She said they rarely saw those actors and that the real competition was happening within Disney, especially when it came to ratings. That's when Romano brought up LaBeouf's feelings about Duff's hugely popular show:

Shia was definitely beefing with Hilary. Hilary had no clue about that. I'm sure she was doing her own thing, but he would always be kind of like, trash-talking Lizzie McGuire. And I was always like, ‘We don't know anything about them.’ Like, why?

The fact that Duff apparently didn't even know there was a rivalry is what gets me. Imagine minding your own business, playing a teenager whose animated alter ego occasionally narrates her problems, and learning decades later that another Disney Channel star was apparently trash-talking your show. That's some remarkably specific after-school drama.

There was a real ratings competition behind it, though. Even Stevens arrived in 2000 and turned LaBeouf's troublemaking Louis Stevens into a breakout character. Lizzie McGuire debuted the following year and quickly became one of the channel's defining hits. Interestingly, Duff's journey to landing the role was pretty wild, though she probably had no idea she'd eventually become part of an alleged rivalry with another Disney star.

Romano suggested the competition mattered especially deeply to LaBeouf, whose childhood and family circumstances had been difficult. She wasn't excusing the comments, exactly, but she offered some perspective on why he might have taken the rivalry so seriously:

He was very competitive. He wanted to be the number one show on the network. He had to be the number one show because I think his life depended on that show doing well. He had a rough upbringing and I think he needed that show to do well for him.

That puts a different spin on Romano's story for me. We're talking about kids carrying two of Disney Channel's biggest shows, and she believes LaBeouf saw Even Stevens as something he couldn't afford to lose. He's spoken about his complicated childhood before, even exploring parts of it in Honey Boy, although he later acknowledged that elements of the film's depiction of his father were fictionalized. Of course, this is Romano's recollection of his behavior more than two decades later, and from the sound of it, Duff didn't even know there was a rivalry.

Romano hasn't exactly sugarcoated her own experience working with LaBeouf, either. In a previous interview, she described their Even Stevens relationship as competitive and sometimes difficult, particularly as the show began focusing more on his character. The two aren't in contact today, although she's said she still wishes him well.

Here's another funny little Disney Channel connection: Romano and Duff actually starred together in the 2002 movie Cadet Kelly, which Duff recently discussed revisiting for a potential sequel. So while LaBeouf was apparently keeping score, his co-star was making movies with the very person he considered competition.

As for Duff, her relationship with Lizzie McGuire has continued long after the original series ended. She's even spoken candidly about Disney's decision to scrap the planned revival, making it clear that she still cares about the character and what the show meant to fans.

Neither Duff nor LaBeouf had publicly responded to Romano's latest claims when the initial reports broke. Still, I know I'll be thinking about this the next time I revisit either show. It's pretty funny to imagine that while the rest of us were flipping between Even Stevens and Lizzie McGuire after school, one of their stars was apparently keeping score the whole time.

Rockstar union agreement covers "pay and bonuses, overtime, redundancies, flexible working, and generative AI policies"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

GTA 6 developers at Rockstar Games will begin the vote on the studio's proposed union right as the new Grand Theft Auto lets players start pre-loading the game on PS5 and Xbox Series X.

News of the impending Rockstar union vote comes from Aftermath, which shared a statement from the Independent Workers' union of Great Britain (IWGB), a labor union with widespread reach including a significant presence in games. IWGB has helped Rockstar developers organize their own studio union to bargain for benefits, rights, and protections.

The voting period will run from November 12 through November 26. GTA 6 launches Thursday, November 19, and pre-loading for the hotly anticipated game starts a week earlier. Rumors indicate GTA 6 is a 210GB download on PS5, so pre-loading ought to come in handy.

While the most-anticipated game of all time is devoured by millions players, many of the people who made it will be charting the future of their workplace. If the vote clears, Rockstar will officially be unionized, which would be a major step forward for the already humming labor push in the broader games industry. Just this month, D&D and Magic The Gathering developers unionized.

IWGB Game Workers shared Aftermath's story online. The agreement, if passed, will "grant workers a say over issues including pay and bonuses, overtime, redundancies, flexible working, and generative AI policies," the union reiterates.

"The terms of the recognition deal, agreed upon by workers and management, would give workers a say over topics including pay and bonuses, overtime, redundancies, flexible working arrangements, and generative AI policies," a press release reads (thanks, Rock Paper Shotgun).

Shanti Easton-Steel, a committee member for the Rockstar Game Workers Union, discussed what's being voted on: "When management choices are kept hidden, we can’t properly address issues like the gender pay gap, the uneven and ever-changing policies on overtime pay, or the concerns many co-workers hold around job security post-release."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

"This is our moment to secure a window onto the decisions that shape our lives, and a seat at the table to improve them. I’m immensely proud of the games Rockstar gives its fans – I want to be equally proud of the voice Rockstar gives its staff," Easton-Steel adds.

This vote follows a messy and ongoing legal dispute over Rockstar staff, including many unionizing staff, who were fired for allegedly leaking "confidential information." Rockstar has repeatedly denied claims of union busting.

Rockstar also has a documented history of crunch, a term often used in game development to describe extended periods of heavy, often under-compensated, and quietly (or loudly) mandated overtime during production – the exact sort of thing that game unions have worked to prevent or control.

Rockstar devs allege crunch is so common at the GTA 6 studio that it's "built into" contracts and you have to "opt out" of it.

#2435. Conferenza Gattuso: "L'unica strada è la serietà e fare le cose a mille allora. Tifosi?..."

📅 Oct 27, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Il mister Gennaro Gattuso è intervenuto in conferenza stampa per commentare il risultato di Sassuolo-Lazio, incontro terminato 2-6

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

"Tanti di questi ragazzi non erano protagonisti, oggi stanno facendo qualcosa di straordinario. A inizio stagione abbiamo provato a fare qualcosa di diverso, smontando la squadra. La prima partita non era andata bene, ma ero tranquillo perché si cominciava a vedere quello che volevamo fare. Ci siamo messi sotto, loro hanno continuato e il segreto è questo. La loro continuità sta migliorando di partita dopo partita, l'unica strada adesso è quella del lavoro. Non guardiamo la classifica, non siamo abituati. L'unica strada è la serietà e fare le cose a mille allora. Oggi abbiamo fatto grandissime cose, sia a sinistra che a destra. Il Sassuolo è forte, ci ha messo in difficoltà, poi siamo stati avvantaggiati anche dall'espulsione".

Quali sono i margini di miglioramento di questa Lazio? La squadra sembrava un tutt'uno con i tifosi...

"Voi fate il vostro mestiere. Per me non sono importanti di gol di Noslin, dobbiamo vedere cosa fa, con quale veemenza va in pressione, va sempre a mille allora. Anche contro il Parma è stato importantissimo. Siamo contenti quando gli attaccanti segnano, questo è importante. Quando non si va a pizzicare e non si va forte, bisogna fare il blocco difensivo. A livello tecnico, tutti stanno facendo robe eccezionali. L'unico limite nostro è andare in avanti e coprire palla, quando la scopriamo siamo vulnerabili e dobbiamo migliorare. I tifosi? Alla squadra l'ho detto, oggi è martedì e c'erano 10mila persone allo stadio. Gli ho detto che è merito loro, per l'attaccamento e per quello che stanno dimostrando. Posso solo ringraziare tutti, è stata una serata incredibile. Quando mi sono rilassato, chiudevo gli occhi e pensavo: 'Pensa che bello quello che stiamo facendo se anche a casa nostra posso vedere una cosa del genere...'. Il loro ritorno? Io ci spero dal primo giorno, abbiamo un obiettivo con i ragazzi e non so se ci riusciremo. Ma facciamo vedere di star onorando questa maglia e di far cambiare idea ai nostri tifosi".

"Sì, qualcuno meriterebbe anche di giocare di più. Ma poi devo fare delle scelte. Oggi me la sono rischiata un po', era giusto fare turnover e ho cambiato solo Diogo Leite. Volevo dare continuità, lavorano con grande veemenza e voglia, meritano tutti di dare minutaggio. Poi bisogna essere bravi perché qualche legnata arriverà, spero il più tardi possibile. Lì vedremo a che livello siamo. Dobbiamo essere bravi. Così l'obiettivo è solo uno, che si fanno le cose con serietà e voglia di lavorare".

Marusic e Rovella sono ancora titolari o faranno fatica? Taylor?

"Taylor l'ho tolto per non rischiare, era pure ammonito. Il livello della partita si stava alzando, per questo l'ho fatto uscire. Poi spero di avere tutti a disposizione, i tre che sono fuori. L'altro giorno Marusic e Rovella hanno fatto qualcosa con noi. Loro stanno vedendo cosa stanno facendo i compagni, ma abbiamo bisogno di tutti. Non mi piace vedere giocatori che lavorano in disparte e in fisioterapia. Poi vediamo".

Questa atmosfera chi l'ha creata? E quanto è importante?

"Io propongo con il mio staff. Sono tanti anni che faccio l'allenatore, se dall'altra parte ci devono essere ragazzi che ti seguono e si fanno voler bene. Ci sono tante componenti, ma la cosa più bella è che tutti si sono messi a disposizione. Ieri la paura più grande era di giocare una partita infrasettimanale, i test dicevano che non avevamo recuperato benissimo. Abbiamo fatto due tre giochi, abbiamo riso per mezz'ora, la partita l'abbiamo preparata in sala video. Ieri dopo l'allenamento abbiamo chiamato i reparti per studiare la partita. A volte fare sempre le stesse cose diventa pesante, loro si divertono così, noi cambiamo spesso allenamento. L'estero mi ha fatto capire che fare sempre le stesse cose non piace ai giocatori, mentalmente si stancano. Noi cerchiamo di andare in questa direzione".

#3444. Invesco brings its model portfolios into Anthropic’s Claude for advisers

📅 Oct 27, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

The $2.5T asset manager joins a growing list of firms plugging their tools into Claude's tool for financial advisers.

Invesco is working with Anthropic to let financial advisers use its model portfolios and practice tools inside Claude for Financial Advisors. CAIS, Conquest and FINNY added their own connectors the same day, a day after Anthropic filed for its IPO.

Invesco is working with Anthropic to bring its model portfolios into Claude, the asset manager said on Tuesday. A new Invesco link, or connector, will let advisers who use its portfolios see that data inside Claude for Financial Advisors.

Anthropic launched its tool for advisers in September, as part of a push into finance that began in May. It hooks Claude up to the portfolio, research and planning tools advisers already use.

The Invesco link also gives advisers its research on how to run and grow their firms. It adds a referral scheme with ready-made scripts. Advisers can use Invesco’s ready-built portfolios or build custom ones with the firm.

Invesco manages $2.5T for clients. Clint Harris runs its solutions and custom strategies unit.

“We are excited to roll out Claude-connectivity, which will allow existing model advisors to have greater access,” he said.

Invesco said the tool is for education only and is not investment advice. It warned that AI answers may be wrong or out of date, and must be checked before anyone relies on them.

Other firms are plugging in too. CAIS, Conquest and FINNY, which make software for advisers, added their own Claude links this week, WealthManagement.com reported. That came a day after Anthropic filed for its IPO.

Anthropic has rivals in the field. London’s MDOTM, whose AI platform is used by Morgan Stanley and Amundi, raised $27M in July.

After Savannah Chrisley announced she's engaged and expecting her first baby, the identity of her mystery fiancé was revealed as Jason Galanis, a businessman Forbes once dubbed as "Porn's New King."

Savannah Chrisley's mystery fiancé has been identified.

After the Chrisley Knows Best alum announced that she's pregnant with her first child, the father of her baby on the way has been revealed as Jason Galanis by multiple outlets.

"There is a huge age gap there," Chrisley shared on the Oct. 27 episode of her Unlocked podcast, explaining that's "probably part of the reason why I kept a lot of it quiet, because I know how brutal the public can be."

The 29-year-old daughter of Todd Chrisley and Julie Chrisley continued, "The age difference—so what? I don't care. He does not look his age, nor does he act his age. His body is great. His mind is even sharper."

Indeed, Jason is 27 years older than Savannah, who most recently dated Robert Shriver for two years before their 2025 breakup. The 56-year-old was notably dubbed as "Porn's New King" by Forbes in 2004 following his purchase of the United States' largest processor of payments for internet porn.

And like Savannah's parents, who were granted clemency by President Donald Trump last year, Jason also has ties to the current commander-in-chief. After all, he, too, made headlines in 2025 when his 14-year prison sentence for his role in two multimillion-dollar fraud schemes received a presidential pardon.

In fact, the parallels between Jason's case and the legal saga involving Savannah's parents—who were convicted on bank fraud and tax evasion charges in 2022—were what led the couple to cross paths. As Savannah put it in her podcast, the two met “in the world of politics" as she was seeking pardons for Todd and Julie.

“When we truly started digging deep into things," Savannah continued, "it was so much stronger of a connection than either of us ever thought was there.”

And that connection led to their engagement last December after five months of dating.

"Jason and I were in the Cayman Islands and little did I know he had a ring in his backpack,” she recalled. “Jason was getting a charger out of his backpack. I think I called him in the other room. He came in there, and then he left a box on the counter. I was like, ‘Oh my god! Is that what I think it is?’ But I didn't know to be 100 percent.”

Jason ended up bringing out the ring after a day at the beach, with Savannah revealing he told her, “‘This can be whatever you want it to be. This can be an engagement ring, a promise ring, a cocktail ring, for all I care. I just want you to know how much I love you.’"

“That proposal was just right. It was everything,” she added. “I would not trade that moment for anything in the entire world because it was us."

"It's more than it's ever happened here."After Julie and Todd went to prison, Savannah gained custody of Grayson and Chloe."I’m not their mom. I’m not their dad. I’m their sister and I get to love and guide them through life," the podcaster wrote on Instagram in July 2023. "Being a bonus parent is TOUGH…no one could ever add up to their parents. But these kiddos have shown me so much love, patience, grace, understanding, and appreciation! Helping to raise these two kiddos is the hardest but most rewarding job I will ever have."And Savannah's bond with Grayson grew even stronger."Many people look at our situation and think, 'She saved him,'" she wrote on Instagram for his 18th birthday in May 2024, "but little do they know… YOU saved ME."

Todd and Julie started out as Chloe's grandparents after his son Kyle fathered the child with ex Angela Johnson in November 2012. However, they adopted her four years later.“My heart!” Julie wrote on Instagram in February 2018. “This child brings so much happiness to our family. What did we do without you?”Fans watched Todd and Julie raise Chloe—or CoCo as her family calls her—on Chrisley Knows Best. But after the couple entered prison, Savannah took over as her guardian.“Watching her grow has been the biggest blessing of my life… she has QUITE the personality!” Savannah wrote on Instagram for Chloe’s 11th birthday in November 2023. "I wish I had her humor. I wish I had her carefree spirit. I wish I had her heart. She is everything that I hope to be one day! There is not a day goes by to where she doesn’t reach me something new. Because of her… we are all better people! I love you sweet girl! KEEP SHINING! NEVER GIVE UP! And ALWAYS KNOW… I AM HERE!”After it was announced that Trump was pardoning Todd and Julie, Savannah shared Chloe’s reaction. "Chloe I think is still in shock, and she doesn't want to get her hopes up because she feels like something bad's going to happen," she said on a May 2025 episode of News Nation. "But I'm excited to be going to get my dad and bringing him home to her."

Faye Chrisley—a.k.a. "Nanny"—is Todd's mom."I am blessed beyond measure that God chose you to be my mother," he wrote on Instagram for Mother's Day in 2021. "I love you more than you will ever know and you fill my heart with love, hope, faith and confidence."Born in September 1944, Nanny grew up in South Carolina. She married army veteran Gene Chrisley, and they welcomed sons Todd, Randy Chrisley and Derrick Chrisley, the latter of whom died when he was a baby. Gene also passed away in 2012.While on Chrisley Knows Best, Nanny captured fans' hearts with her humor, fun times with sister Frances (who died in 2022), dating adventures and advice. And whether she was hitting the casino, raising a glass of wine or spending time with family, she proved to viewers she knows how to have a good time.However, Nanny has gone through hard times too. In addition to Todd and Julie's convictions, Nanny was diagnosed with bladder cancer in 2021. But two years later, she shared she had overcome her health battle."I’m in remission, thank God," Nanny said on a 2023 episode of Lindsie's podcast The Southern Tea, per People. "I’ve been out moving around, doing the best I can."Doing the best she can has been Nanny's approach to life in general."The world don’t always give you a good deck of cards to play with, so you play with them the best you can," she said on Savannah's podcast Unlocked in 2023. "You get up, brush yourself off and keep going."
